body: In 2018, as self-driving cars started rolling cautiously through the streets of Silicon Valley and select cities,
Stanford’s own experts said

we were 90 percent of the way to a driverless future. But that last 10 percent proved stubborn. While tech optimists were promising self-sufficient planes, trucks, and cars, researchers were still trying to figure out how these vehicles could see through fog and rain, navigate using street markings of varying styles and quality, and learn safe decision-making.
Cut to today: Cars without drivers – or even without a driver’s seat – are now operating routinely in several cities, including in the San Francisco Bay Area.
“After approximately 20 years of development, AV technology is really becoming part of our daily lives,” said
Marco Pavone
, associate professor of aeronautics and astronautics in the
School of Engineering
Marco Pavone | Rod Searcey
Pavone, who is director of the
Autonomous Systems Laboratory
and the
Sustainable Mobility Center
, has been in the thick of autonomous robotic research and development. He shared insights about what has gotten this technology across the finish line and what to expect next.
Where are we with autonomous vehicle technology?

Here in the Bay Area and San Francisco, robotaxi services are becoming quite mainstream, not just in the cities but also in the suburbs. They aren’t providing the majority of ridership across the United States yet, but if you go to San Francisco, chances are you will see one. Advanced automated technologies, such as autopilot, are becoming mainstream on consumer vehicles as well.
This is one of the most complex technologies that humankind has developed, so it took quite some time to perfect it. But there has been an acceleration lately, and AI has been key.

AI has accelerated progress across the development cycle. It advanced the software on the vehicle and also improved all the processes that are necessary to build that software, such as curating data for model training, improving the fidelity of simulation, and automating evaluations of the vehicle’s performance.
What’s one way AI has made driverless cars more road-ready?

To enable autonomy, cars have software stacks that address and coordinate – either explicitly or implicitly – various tasks, like object detection, object tracking, planning, control, and decision-making. In the past few years, there’s been a shift from engineers manually coding individual pieces of software and integrating them into a cohesive stack toward increasingly data-driven and end-to-end systems. Neural networks now play a much larger role across the stack, with models increasingly learning from large-scale driving data, including demonstrations collected from human drivers.

This change has been proven very useful in a number of ways. First of all, the ceiling for data-driven approaches is much higher: With more high-quality and diverse data, these systems can continue to improve. Also, some tasks are very hard for engineers to recreate from scratch. Whereas, if the vehicle learns from human demonstrations, the driving is more likely to align with how humans actually drive.
What are some of the toughest problems to solve when it comes to AV technology?
Two key bottlenecks are deploying autonomous vehicle systems more widely and validating the safety of these systems – without requiring excessive amounts of new data.

Robot autonomy means developing robotic systems that can work in situations that cannot be foreseen at the design stage; systems that can reason about complex situations in some intelligent way. As we try to design for more and rarer situations, it becomes increasingly expensive and harder for human designers to conceptualize those. So, you’re basically relying on driving so many miles that virtually every situation can be experienced and taught to the system.

As for safety, you don’t just want a system that is safe and robust, you also have to prove to yourself and to the community that it is safe and dependable. To do that, you need technologies that can robustly validate the system with an attainable amount of data.

One of the new, exciting developments to address both challenges has been leveraging internet-pretrained models. I compare this to a human learning how to drive: When you’re practicing for your driver’s license, you rely on 16 years of experience gained through tasks not related to driving – being a passenger, being a pedestrian, improving your reaction time through sports, etc. – that scaffold the core capabilities needed to become a good driver. That’s why, depending on the state, you can qualify for a driver’s license with only tens of hours of supervised driving practice. Similarly, internet-pretrained models can leverage knowledge acquired from a vast range of tasks that are not directly related to driving.

This provides the vehicle with a broad base of prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities, so that driving-specific data can be used to specialize the model rather than teach it everything from scratch. In other words, by leveraging experience from the broader internet, we can substantially reduce the amount of driving data needed to make the vehicle a capable driver. This can also help with safety validation – for example, by generating challenging yet plausible scenarios that can be used to stress-test the vehicle and uncover failure modes that may be difficult to discover from driving data alone.
What’s next for autonomous vehicle technology?

Automated technologies are a spectrum. In the next two or three years, we will see advanced automated technologies deployed across nearly every type of vehicle beyond passenger cars: trucks, construction machines, agricultural machines, low-speed shuttles, and the various vehicles that move people in airports. So, even though we are witnessing automated technologies most visibly in the context of personal mobility, it is going to be widespread – and this is happening as we speak. These technologies will make vehicles safer and more comfortable.

The big next question is: Where else are we going to see robotic systems? Humanoids? Quadrupeds? The timeline for such things will be much more varied, given the significant fragmentation of the robotics ecosystem across tasks, embodiments, and industries. But it’s plausible that, sooner rather than later, this new wave of robotics will find viable applications and begin to reach significant economic scale.
The road to autonomy
With safety as a guiding principle, Stanford research has long advanced the science of autonomous driving. Here’s a look back at some of the ideas and experiments behind that progress.
Testing the limits with a drifting DeLorean
Engineers built MARTY, a self-driving research vehicle, to study the ways cars handle extreme situations.
Understanding the handoff to human drivers
Researchers tested how drivers adjusted their steering when retaking control under changed conditions.
Giving robots a wider view
Stanford and UC San Diego researchers developed a wide-angle 4D camera with potential applications in autonomous vehicles and other robotic systems.
Connecting space robotics and self-driving cars
Marco Pavone explored how algorithms for robots in space could help autonomous vehicles navigate changing environments on Earth.
Seeing around corners
Researchers developed a laser-based imaging technique to reveal hidden objects, with potential applications for detecting road hazards.
Coordinating two driverless cars in a tandem drift
Stanford and Toyota Research Institute researchers demonstrated autonomous tandem drifting to explore ways AI could improve driving safety.
A Stanford professor and his students transformed a vintage 1981 DeLorean into a high-performance test bed for researching the physical limits of autonomous driving. | Aaron Kehoe
For more information

Precourt Institute for Energy
, a faculty affiliate of the
Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI)
, and a member of the
Institute for Computational and Mathematical Engineering (ICME)

body: In brief
Small proteins, called peptides, could be an excellent tool to kill harmful bacteria without causing antibiotic resistance because they destroy bacteria physically, rather than chemically.
The problem is that peptides are short-lived and expensive to work with.

So, Stanford researchers have developed an AI-assisted tool that predicts polymers that have similar antimicrobial characteristics to peptides. They chose these chain-like molecules because they are inexpensive, easy to work with, don’t degrade quickly, and are very safe.
Using the tool, they found and tested polymer candidates for antimicrobial properties against E. coli bacteria. They found 10 candidates that performed well above expectations.
The researchers are hopeful the tool could be useful to find a variety of new microbe-specific drugs, including some to address especially challenging bacterial infections.

Swimming in the blood, sweat, cells, and tears of every human are small proteins known as peptides. Many peptides can kill bacteria on contact, and yet the bacteria never seem to evolve resistance to them. Mass-produced peptides could become a new type of resistance-evading antibiotics, but peptides are a challenging partner. They are short-lived and expensive to synthesize.
In a
new paper
, researchers at
Stanford School of Engineering

describe how they have trained an AI model to scour millions of potential other molecules – polymers – for candidates that mimic the mechanisms peptides use to kill bacteria so effectively. These new polymers also share the peptides’ ability to overcome or escape the microbial resistance that plagues many traditional antibiotics, bringing hope to the public health community. Millions worldwide die each year from microbial infections resistant or immune to existing medications.

“Antimicrobial peptides are chemically able to get very close to and disrupt the cell membrane, killing the bacteria,” explained Shoshana Williams, a former graduate student chemist at Stanford Engineering who recently earned her PhD working on this challenge. “Importantly, they don’t need to get inside the cell to work, like a typical drug would. Nor do they work on one specific protein or pathway, like drugs do.”
The key to evading resistance is that these new molecules use a physical, rather than a biochemical, pathway to attack the bacteria.
“The peptides
permeabilize
the microbes … they literally rip holes in the cell membrane to kill them,” interjected
Eric Appel

, a professor of materials science and senior author of the study. “It’s much harder for a bacterium to change the entire lipid structure of its membrane or the electrical charge of its surface than to learn to reject a chemical drug or turn off its narrow pathway.”
Uncertainty principles

The researchers are quick to point out that the new chemicals are not synthetic peptides, but rather a different type of molecule altogether: polymers. These long, chain-like molecules are easier and cheaper to synthesize than peptides and do not degrade easily, enabling global distribution and access to low-resource communities. Polymers are also “super safe,” Appel added.

The researchers built a library of 1.7 million potential polymer candidates to choose from – an overwhelming number to investigate manually, so they did it computationally. They developed a new model that predicts the chemical properties of the polymers based on their chemical structures and identifies those that have similar antimicrobial characteristics to the peptides.
Left: Unperturbed bacteria. Right: Bacteria exhibiting damaged cell membranes after treatment with an antimicrobial polymer. | Changxin Dong and Shoshana Williams
Here the researchers ran into a challenge that afflicts many areas of medical AI: a lack of data. Large datasets exist for antimicrobial
peptides

, but those for polymers are scarce. “The dataset of antimicrobial polymers simply was nowhere near big enough,” said Williams, who is now a postdoctoral scholar at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. “With a chemist’s intuition, however, we pivoted to train on the chemical properties of antimicrobial peptides first and applied that knowledge to the polymers. It worked!”
Leaps and bounds

One strategy the team developed to overcome the dearth of data was clever – and counterintuitive. It was based on uncertainty. They started by asking a bunch of models to predict which polymers would perform best, but instead of simply accepting the polymers that the majority of the models agreed upon, the team looked only where there was the greatest
disagreement
between models.

“We figured that if you want to improve the models, it’s really a good space to feed in more actual experimental data,” Williams explained. The team synthesized the 20 most disputed candidates, where some models thought the polymers would be excellent and others thought they would be terrible antibiotics. Then, they tested them and fed that data back into the models to supplement the polymer dataset.
“At this point, we had a much more robust system able to select the greatest hits from among the polymers in the library,” Williams said.

“The primary intellectual leap was training on the antimicrobial peptide data first and then to use that data to make predictions on the polymers, an entirely different class of molecules," Appel said. “There are thousands of peptides that have been evaluated where all of the chemical content is known. We just ‘featurized’ each one of those and connected them to standardized data outputs for the polymers.”
With their new, more robust AI tool, the team was able to narrow the list of polymer candidates to just 10 that were then synthesized and tested for antimicrobial properties. In tests on
E. coli

bacteria, all ten candidates performed well above expectations and one proved particularly effective against biofilms – a challenging type of microbial community that is difficult to treat with conventional antibiotics.
“These 10 candidates are among the most potent antimicrobial polymers ever reported, as far as I’m aware,” Williams said.
Above and beyond

Beyond an impressive proof-of-concept molecular design process, Appel and Williams think the system could prove effective in designing microbe-specific drugs. They tested their approach primarily against
E. coli
, which belongs to a class of double-membraned microbes, called Gram-negative bacteria, that includes salmonella and cholera.
“We haven’t had a new class of antibiotics against Gram-negatives in decades,” Williams pointed out. “But it also works against Gram-positive bacteria, like
Staphylococcus aureus,
as well.”
Appel can imagine designing bespoke antibiotic polymers that kill only the strains of bacteria causing an infection, leaving human tissue and good bacteria unharmed.

“We really do need better drugs,” Appel concluded. “This new process opens a promising path to identifying novel antibiotics that work in new and different ways to treat serious and complicated infections and combat resistance.”
For more information

Contributing Stanford University authors include: graduate students Anna Makar-Limanov, Gabriel Greenstein, Priya Ganesh, Noah Eckman, Changxin Dong; post-doctoral scholars Xinyu Liu, Alessio Fragasso, Alexander N. Prossnitz, and Hector Lopez Hernandez; and professors
Christine Jacobs-Wagner
, the Dennis Cunningham Professor in the Department of Biology in the School of Humanities and Sciences (H&S) and professor of microbiology and immunology in the School of Medicine, and
Lynette Cegelski
, professor of chemistry in H&S.
Appel is also a member of
Stanford Bio-X
, the
Cardiovascular Institute
, the
Wu Tsai Human Performance Alliance
, the
Maternal & Child Health Research Institute (MCHRI)
Stanford Cancer Institute
, and the
Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute
, and a faculty fellow at
Sarafan ChEM-H

. Cegelski is also a member of Bio-X and the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute, and a faculty fellow at Sarafan ChEM-H. Jacbos-Wagner is also a member of Bio-X and an institute scholar at Sarafan ChEM-H.

This work was funded by the Stanford Bio-X Interdisciplinary Initiative Seed Grants Program, by the National Institute of General Medical Sciences of the National Institutes of Health, and work was performed at the Stanford Nano Shared Facilities (SNSF), supported by the National Science Foundation.

body: An extraordinarily large and well-preserved fossilized mastodon tooth, discovered this summer in a creek bed in the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen), has been donated to Stanford University. The enormous molar belonged to a Pacific mastodon, a species from the Pleistocene of western North America newly described and officially recognized in 2019.

Unlike the ground sloths, mammoths, camels, pronghorn antelopes, and bison, which grazed in grassy fields in this area, the Pacific mastodon browsed on the leaves of trees in shaded riparian environments. The fossil is being preserved for carbon dating, 3D imaging, and further study in the Geoscience Specimen Collection.

Geomorphologist Brigid Lynch discovered a mastodon tooth in a creek bed while working on a project to improve habitat for the threatened California red-legged frog. The unexpected find prompted a collaboration to identify and preserve the fossil. | Balance Hydrologics via Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District

Matt Sharp Chaney of the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District and Stanford Libraries curator Chrissy Garcia hold the fossil in front of artwork at the district’s offices. Now part of Stanford’s Geoscience Specimen Collection, the fossil supports research into Bay Area Ice Age animals and ecosystems. | Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District

Tony Calavano of Stanford Libraries’ Digital Library Systems and Services department scans the mastodon tooth. Digitization allows students, researchers, and the public to explore the fossil beyond the collection’s walls. | Stanford University Libraries

A measuring tape puts the enormous molar’s size in perspective. Further study, including planned carbon dating, could help researchers place this individual mastodon in the region’s ecological history. | Stanford University Libraries
Previous
Next
Close
“Fossils such as this tooth are critical for understanding what species lived in this area prior to and during early human occupation,” said
Jonathan Payne

, the Dorrell William Kirby Professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences. “They help us assess what a pre-human baseline ecosystem looked like and how we might restore aspects of it, if we wanted to. The fossils teach us more broadly the geography of ancient species and the timing of their extinction so that we can learn how species have responded to climate change in the past and might do so in the future.”

“But for thinking about this specific tooth” added Payne, “there’s also the key difference between the idea of a mastodon and the experience of holding the tooth of one particular mastodon that lived its life where I am now living mine. Mammoths and mastodons, like elephants, were undoubtedly smart and social animals that experienced love for their parents, offspring, siblings, and friends and that were curious about the world around them. They are also a reminder that the world was not always the way it is today and, by extension, we have the ability to make the future different from and better than today if we make wise choices.”

Brigid Lynch, a geomorphologist with Balance Hydrologics, discovered the fossil while working on a Midpen project to enhance habitat for the threatened California red-legged frog. She and her colleagues contacted Garret Trask, senior archaeologist for Stanford Heritage Services, for assistance in identifying and preserving the fossil while Midpen explored the best course of action for its long-term care. News of the remarkable find was also shared with Wayne Thompson, owner of Pacific Paleontology, and Chrissy Garcia, curator and manager of Stanford’s Geoscience Specimen Collection. Ultimately, Midpen donated it to Stanford and issued the first published report, “
Rare Fossil Found in Midpen Preserve
,” in its newsletter.

In the Midpen report, Garcia stated, “Fossils are our only opportunity to see into past biodiversity. We can study fossils to better understand Earth’s past … and to make better predictions and better decisions about how to help our ecosystems and biodiversity thrive into the future.”
Garcia collaborated with the Libraries’ Digitization Services Lab to create a 3D scan and print of the fossil for teaching and outreach purposes. A copy of the scan is now available via the
Stanford Digital Repository

. Her role exemplifies the broader efforts of Stanford’s librarians to contribute their conservation skills, subject knowledge, and expertise in cataloging and collection management to raise awareness of the special collections and archives assembled by academic departments and centers since the university’s founding, and to make them widely available.
For more information

by Stanford University Libraries.

body: In brief
Stanford Medicine researchers discovered the human brain comprises two separately evolved organs, overturning the long-held single-origin developmental model.
The scientists identified two distinct progenitor cells in mouse embryos and traced the two-origin brain pattern across 550 million years of evolution.
The scientists produced functional human hindbrain motor neurons in the laboratory, supporting future research on SMA, ALS, and other brain-stem disorders.
For centuries, scientists have thought of the
brain
as a single, unified organ. But new research led by Stanford Medicine reveals that what we call the brain is two distinct organs that evolved independently over hundreds of millions of years.

The discovery overturns a prevailing model of brain development. For decades researchers have subscribed to the theory that there is a single progenitor cell early in development that gives rise to the entire brain. This model suggested all parts of the brain shared a common developmental origin.

The new research finding shows that the human brain consists of two ancient nervous systems cleverly packaged together – a more primitive part that regulates our hearts’ beating, our breathing, and other functions, and another that makes us distinctly human, capable of poetry, mathematics, and wondering about our own origins.

The discovery could help explain why scientists have struggled for decades to grow certain types of brain cells in the laboratory – and it opens new avenues for studying devastating diseases that affect the brain stem, such as spinal muscular atrophy (also known as SMA) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (also known as ALS or Lou Gehrig’s disease).
“We’ve shown for the first time that the front of the brain arises from a totally different progenitor cell than the back of the brain,” said
Kyle Loh
, PhD, associate professor of developmental biology. “Our discovery means that we can now grow neurons from the back of the brain, the hindbrain, in a petri dish and study their functions.”
The
findings
were published in
Nature Neuroscience
Sept. 18. Loh is the senior author. Graduate students Carolyn Dundes and Rayyan Jokhai are co-first authors of the research.
Two brains

The adult brain has three main regions: the forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain. The forebrain handles higher-level thinking – language, consciousness, and abstract reasoning. In contrast, the hindbrain, located at the back of the skull and often called the brain stem, controls essential, automatic functions that keep us alive: breathing, sleeping, and regulating our heartbeat and hunger urges. The hindbrain neurons also control the muscles of the face, tongue, and throat, which affect speech and swallowing.

Despite the critical importance of the hindbrain, scientists have struggled for decades to generate human hindbrain neurons in the laboratory. This gap has hampered research into devastating diseases affecting the brain stem, including spinal muscular atrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

SMA is a leading genetic cause of death in children under 1 year of age. ALS, which is often diagnosed between the ages of 40 and 70, affects both the forebrain and the hindbrain. In both disorders, certain hindbrain neurons gradually cease to function, and the patient loses the ability to swallow, which can cause pneumonia when food or liquid is inhaled into the lungs; eventually, patients lose the ability to breathe.
We’ve shown for the first time that the front of the brain arises from a totally different progenitor cell than the back of the brain.
Kyle Loh
Associate Professor of Developmental Biology

The researchers’ breakthrough came from studying the earliest moments of embryonic development, during a stage called gastrulation, when the body first takes shape. Jokhai and Dundes discovered that the hindbrain follows a separate developmental path, running in parallel to – rather than branching off from – the pathway that creates the forebrain and midbrain.

The researchers learned this from examining developing mouse embryos. They identified two different brain progenitor cells. One, which expresses a gene called Otx2, is destined to become the forebrain and midbrain. The other, which expresses a gene called Gbx2, is committed to forming the hindbrain. They showed that these two cell populations never overlap; they are mutually exclusive from the earliest stages of development.

The team then examined the DNA packaging, or chromatin, in these cells. Chromatin is a way cells determine which genes can be easily accessed and which are bundled away out of reach. What they found was striking: The anterior neural ectoderm (future forebrain and midbrain) and posterior neural ectoderm (future hindbrain) have fundamentally different chromatin configurations. These differences essentially locked each progenitor cell into its respective fate, like travelers on parallel tracks that never cross.
“Previous attempts to make hindbrain neurons likely tried to coax forebrain and midbrain progenitors into hindbrain cells, which our study shows is not possible,” Jokhai said.
This revelation explained decades of frustration in the field — scientists had been trying to turn one type of progenitor cell into another that it is fundamentally incapable of becoming.

“In stem cell biology, people are always fixated with creating the end cell type, like the neuron,” Jokhai said. “But it’s important to begin at the earliest stages of embryonic development. Our careful attention to that early time point allowed us to find this fundamental split in brain development.”
Growing hindbrain neurons

Armed with this knowledge, the researchers for the first time successfully coaxed human pluripotent stem cells (a kind of cell that can create any cell in the human body) to become functional hindbrain motor neurons in the laboratory. These lab-grown neurons displayed all the hallmarks of authentic hindbrain cells: They exhibited waves of electrical activity called action potentials and made proteins that identify the segments of the hindbrain that control facial and swallowing muscles.

Finally, the researchers looked back over 550 million years of evolutionary time. They found the same two-origin brain pattern in chickens; zebrafish; and, remarkably, in acorn worms, tiny creatures living on the ocean floor that share a distant common ancestor with humans. Jellyfish, which diverged from humans about 600 to 700 million years ago, have two nervous systems at different ends of their body.

“Our research suggests that evolution took two existing neural systems and pushed them together spatially,” Loh said. “Having the brain as one organ would probably be more efficient, but we rely on this primordial way to make the brain as two separate pieces.”

“I was surprised at our findings because the word ‘brain’ implies a contiguous organ that likely has a singular origin,” Jokhai said. “But even 500 million years ago, there were these separate neural systems, which now almost operate as one, which is very cool.”

The research also has implications for investigating treatments for SMA, ALS, and other conditions affecting the brain stem. Until now, studying these diseases has been nearly impossible because scientists cannot obtain brain stem tissue from living patients. The ability to grow these neurons in a dish opens new possibilities for understanding what goes wrong. There’s even an unexpected connection to obesity treatment: The hindbrain contains circuits that regulate hunger – which is precisely how weight-loss drugs like semaglutide work.
The researchers would like to extend their studies to determine the developmental origins of the spinal cord and to learn exactly how SMA and ALS compromise the function of hindbrain neurons.
“Now we have a model to better understand these devastating diseases, and work toward regenerative therapies for them,” Jokhai said. “This is a very exciting new frontier in brain research.”
For more information
Researchers from the California Institute of Technology and the University of California, San Francisco, contributed to the study.

body: Kenneth Schultz, the William Bennett Munro Professor of Political Science, says education is “an inherently global enterprise.”
On Sept. 1, Schultz became the Burke Family Director of the
Bing Overseas Studies Program (BOSP)

. A longtime BOSP faculty partner who earned his PhD in political science at Stanford in 1996, he has served on BOSP’s Faculty Oversight and Executive Committees and participated in six reviews of overseas centers and programs.
He shares how he hopes to guide the program’s next chapter and why he thinks the opportunity to study abroad is one of the most valuable aspects of the Stanford experience.
What drew you to the program and what excites you about this new role?

I have been involved in BOSP since 2008, when I served as faculty in residence in Florence. At the time, I was the director of the International Relations program, the only major on campus that requires all of its students to spend a quarter studying abroad. I had seen how important the overseas experience was to our majors, and I wanted to get more involved and learn about the program firsthand. I did a second stint as a faculty in residence in Oxford in 2012, and have since served on every BOSP faculty committee and helped review most of its programs.

I have invested so much in BOSP because I believe in its mission and think it’s one of the gems of a Stanford experience. Study abroad is a key part of a liberal education, and I am excited by the opportunity to lead and shape this program in its next chapter.
What makes study abroad so important?

As a professor of international relations, I think it’s essential for our students to engage meaningfully with the world outside our borders. It gives you a chance not only to learn about different countries but also to see your own country from a different perspective. Particularly now, when global politics feel fraught and longstanding assumptions about the United States’ role in the world are being debated, we need to equip our students to be part of the conversation. This is not just about preparing the next generation of policymakers or diplomats, but about helping students become informed citizens, prepared to engage with the world through science, engineering, art and literature, business, or whatever path they choose.

I spent the past academic year on sabbatical at ETH Zurich, a world-class university in Switzerland. My time there reinforced my belief that the core mission of universities – the production and dissemination of knowledge – is an inherently global enterprise. My research is related to conflicts over borders between states, and it was thought-provoking to live and travel in a country with a fascinating history shaped by different languages, geography, and foreign influences. It also reminded me how living abroad helps us grow intellectually and personally. From interacting with colleagues from different countries to figuring out how to navigate the public transit system, you encounter new ideas, exercise different parts of your brain, and see the different ways other countries approach familiar problems.
What opportunities do you see for the program in the future?

I want to make sure that our program makes sense given the world we live in and what our students want and need from overseas studies, while always centering the core values of academic rigor and cultural engagement. Part of that is integrating new topics into our curriculum, such as sustainability or data science. It also involves updating curricula to take advantage of what makes each location distinctive today. We are also looking at strengthening and expanding internship opportunities, so that more students can combine study abroad with work abroad. A continuing priority is finding ways to make study away available to students who might otherwise struggle to fit it into their schedules. The summer global seminars play an important role there, providing an intensive experience outside of the normal academic year and allowing us to expand the range of locations we offer. Finally, with the expansion of the
COLLEGE
curriculum to include a required global perspectives quarter, there is an opportunity to get every student thinking early on about how a global experience can be part of their education.
What do you hope students will gain from their study away experience?

Our students know that studying away is a special opportunity, but I want to make sure they understand the true nature of the opportunity BOSP offers. This is a chance not just to travel but to engage deeply, both academically and culturally, with their host city, country, and region. It’s seeing amazing sights and tasting interesting food, yes, but it’s also learning about and navigating an unfamiliar culture – in some cases a new language – and thinking about why different societies do things differently from what they are used to. It will take them out of their familiar routines in ways that may sometimes be a little disorienting. That’s a feature, not a bug. In fact, studies have shown that living abroad can lead to increased creativity and resilience.

Our students come from very diverse backgrounds. Some have little experience with international travel, and others came to Stanford from abroad. So different students will take something different from study away. But I hope that every student experiences intellectual and personal growth, which could manifest in any number of ways after they come home. That could mean further coursework, a project, a new hobby, or even just greater confidence in going someplace new.

body: The interaction between online life and teens’ mental health keeps hitting the news. In August, Meta agreed to pay $17 billion to settle a federal lawsuit over addictive features of Facebook and Instagram targeted toward youth. On Sept. 10, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a
new law
banning addictive social media features for those younger than 16. And several states are adding
health warnings
to social media platforms for youth; California’s takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

But as mental health experts, policymakers, parents, and educators grapple with how to help teenagers stay safe online, they’ve run into a significant challenge: Online experiences aren’t a monolith, yet research on teens’ online lives tends to focus on only a few platforms or harms at a time.
Stanford University experts and their colleagues aim to fill the data gap via a comprehensive survey about what specific harms occur on each major online platform and whom they most affect.
“If we’re not measuring how often these specific harms are happening, or what our kids are actually experiencing online, we have no way of knowing whether an intervention is working,” said
Eleni Linos
, MD, DrPH, director of the
Stanford Center for Digital Health
and a professor at Stanford Medicine. “In order to know if a specific harm is decreasing, we need to show this with actual data.”
The new
study
, published Sept. 18 in
JAMA Pediatrics
, offers one of the first comprehensive attempts to survey teens about the harms they experience online.

The research team shared key insights from their survey of a nationally representative sample of U.S. 13- to 17-year-olds who were asked about their online and offline experiences of several forms of harm over the previous four weeks. So far, the researchers have collected pilot data from 472 participants. They envision this research as a starting point for asking the same questions of much larger groups of teens.
Here are five takeaways from their work.
1. Measuring several specific harms, from many platforms, gives better insight into what teens experience online

Understanding online harms requires considering how different people experience many kinds of harms on various online platforms. The team at the Stanford Center for Digital Health reviewed past work and convened experts from academia, tech companies, and advocacy and mental health organizations to develop an extensive list of potential harms to ask teens about. In the survey they developed, some questions were worded broadly – “Have you personally witnessed or experienced something that affected you negatively?” and “Have you witnessed or experienced content that you would consider bad for the world?”

Other questions were specific, such as asking about exposure to unwanted sexual images; content that made someone feel worse about themselves; insults or threats; violent images; content that encouraged self-harm; or content that discriminated against people based on gender, religion, race, sexual orientation, or other aspects of identity.

The survey asked about experiences of each harm on many platforms, including several types of social media, Pinterest, Discord (a free online communication platform that can be used for texts, voice calls, and video chats), online gaming, text messages, FaceTime, and email. They also asked how frequently each online activity disrupted participants’ sleep.

“We thought it was important to ask about each of these distinct kinds of harms separately, and across platforms,” said lead study author Angela Lee, PhD, who was a postdoctoral scholar at the Stanford Center for Digital Health when the study was conducted. “This lets us go beyond broad statements like, ‘Being online is bad,’ to understanding the specific places where adolescents are saying that they are having bad experiences.”

The researchers also collected detailed demographic information about each participant to allow them to identify which harms are most likely to crop up for which teens and whether external social factors contribute to negative experiences.
If we’re not measuring how often these specific harms are happening, we have no way of knowing whether an intervention is working.
Eleni Linos
Professor of Dermatology and of Medicine
2. Teens’ online experiences are extremely varied
“Our results showed that teens reported experiencing more harms on certain platforms,” Lee said.

Rates of reported sleep disruption attributed to specific apps ranged from single digits to around 40%, depending on the platform, with a total of about half of participants reporting that at least one aspect of their online activities had “sometimes” or “often” disrupted their sleep in the previous four weeks.

Teens’ rates of experiencing bullying or harassment ranged from near zero to around 8%, depending on the platform, with the highest rates in certain apps that enable messaging. Rates of witnessing bullying or harassment of others were generally higher than rates of experiencing bullying personally, but they also varied widely among platforms.

Because the study sample is relatively small, it’s too early to know to what degree differences in negative experiences are due to the platforms versus who is using them, the paper noted. “For example, exposure to content that makes one feel bad about oneself was more prevalent on Pinterest than on Discord. While this could reflect stronger content moderation policies or safer design on Discord, it could also reflect Pinterest’s greater popularity among girls, who may be more susceptible to social comparison than boys,” the authors wrote.

“Future work is needed to disentangle how much of these differences in reported harms are driven by user selection or the dynamics of engagement with the platform, in addition to considering how people interact with different platforms,” Lee said.
3. Teens’ online experiences need to be compared with what they experience in the rest of life

This important control question – how rates of online harms compare with the prevalence of the same harm offline – hasn’t always been included in previous surveys of what teens experience online. As anyone who was a teenager before the 2000s can tell you, teens found ways to treat each other poorly before the internet existed.

Some forms of harm occur about as often online and offline, the study found: Direct harassment was about as common in both places, with 18.5% of teens reporting they had been harassed offline versus 16.4% online in the previous four weeks.
But other forms of harm were much more common online, including exposure to violent imagery, unwanted sexual images, and content that encouraged self-harm.

The gaps between online and offline experiences can help point toward the largest opportunities to make online life better, the researchers said. Some forms of harm – such as when teens are sexually solicited online – clearly point to a need for better responses to online risks from the legal system and other structures designed to protect young people.
4. Navigating the mix of online and offline life makes it a challenging time to be a kid
“I want teens to know that the harms and risks they encounter online are not acceptable,” said study co-author
Sunny Xun Liu
, PhD, director of research for the
Social Media Lab
within Stanford University’s Department of Communication. “We want them to grow up in a digital world where they feel safe to explore.”

Liu said she hopes teens will always feel willing to share what they see and experience online, particularly as it relates to telling adults about emerging harms or risks they face on new platforms where they are among the earliest adopters.
“Teens are often the first to encounter new risks and harms related to technology, especially artificial intelligence,” she said. “Their insights will help us identify and mitigate those problems.”
5. It’s a tricky time to be a parent as well
Until now, discussions on how parents can mitigate online harms have often taken broad strokes, such as encouraging parents to limit total screen time or sign up for campaigns like
Wait Until 8th
, in which families commit to keeping their children cellphone-free until eighth grade.

“It can be hard for parents to know where it is safe for their kids to play and explore online,” Lee said. “We hope we can get a more granular look at where harms are concentrated. I think it’s also important to recognize that there are both serious harms and meaningful benefits to being online for many young people.”

For example, she said, online communities can be supportive spaces for teens from marginalized groups, and most teens feel benefits from staying in touch with friends and peers through different communication channels.

“As we keep supporting youth safety online, I hope we can keep open connections with teens in our lives: asking them what they see online; how it makes them feel; and helping support them if they have experiences that are scary, hurtful, or problematic.”
For more information
Researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, New York University, and the University of Southern California contributed to the study.
This story was
originally published
by Stanford Medicine.

body: In brief
Stanford scientists have confirmed the long-predicted ability of quantum units of sound, or “phonons,” to suddenly change energy levels.
The team created a device that takes hundreds of measurements within two milliseconds to pinpoint the moment of a quantum jump.
The advance has implications for quantum computing and sensing, as well as for improving everyday technologies, such as smartphones.
A Stanford team has documented the first direct observation of quantum jumps of sound in a mechanical resonator, completing an arc of scientific exploration that started over a hundred years ago.

Quantum jumps – sudden transitions from one energy state to another – have been theorized since the early 1900s. Scientists first demonstrated these jumps in trapped ions in 1986 and later in photons, the fundamental particles of light, in 2007. Observing quantum jumps of sound had remained elusive, but a team led by Stanford physicist Amir Safavi-Naeini has recorded these phenomena, publishing the findings in the journal
Science
“What this study shows will allow us to move forward with developing new quantum technologies with sound,” said
Safavi-Naeini
, associate professor of applied physics in the Stanford
School of Humanities and Sciences
. “We have seen that vibrating objects can exhibit quantum behavior, which is the prerequisite for many of the operations needed by quantum computing and sensing.”
While a quantum unit of light – its smallest possible discrete piece – is a singular photon, a quantum unit of sound, or “phonon,” represents the coordinated movement of a large group of atoms.

To the human senses, vibrating motion from sound, like that seen in a struck bell, appears to decline gradually rather than make an abrupt jump to stillness. At the quantum level, however, a resonator’s vibrational energy changes in discrete steps, or jumps, similar to the quantum behavior of ions and photons. Earlier experiments had found evidence of these jumps, but this study is the first to demonstrate individual phonons making quantum jumps in real time.
Size and timing
The mechanical resonator was fabricated using chipmaking techniques. It is so small that many resonators could be packed onto a chip to perform complex functions.

The length of time the resonator can “ring” is what made this breakthrough possible. Working sort of like a microscopic tuning fork, the resonator can vibrate for two milliseconds. For comparison, if the same capability were found in a regular-sized tuning fork, it would ring for several hours.

The long resonation, or “ringdown time,” of the resonator allowed for hundreds of readings to be taken to determine the moment the vibration was no longer present and the sound jumped – when it moved from an energy state of 1 to 0.
What this study shows will allow us to move forward with developing new quantum technologies with sound.
Amir Safavi-Naeini
Associate Professor of Applied Physics
Sound control
To conduct this experiment, the researchers had to overcome an ongoing challenge in quantum engineering: how to get a signal out of a quantum system without disturbing its fragile state.

Takuma Makihara and Erik Szakiel, the co-first authors on the study, developed a way to pair the microscopic mechanical resonator with a superconducting qubit, an electrical circuit that can store quantum information and serve as a detector

“We had to continually develop new processes to make this extremely long-lived, vibrating object and then integrate it with the qubit, which is our little electrical detector – without ruining either subsystem,” said Makihara, a recent Stanford doctoral graduate.

The qubit can read out what is happening in the mechanical resonator, essentially checking over and over during the two milliseconds of vibration if the phonon inside is at an energy level of 1 or at 0. This is how the researchers can record the moment a quantum jump occurs.
Developing a sound platform
This study represents a foundational first step, but the ability to detect quantum jumps of sound could lead to a number of advances.

It could help solve the error correction problem in quantum computing, for instance. While quantum computing holds great potential for handling some complex calculations beyond the capacity of traditional computers, fragile quantum states can cause errors before a calculation is finished. In many quantum computing architectures, a quantum jump represents an error, but identifying when those occur has been difficult. So the ability to detect quantum jumps in sound marks an important step toward error correction.

Because of its small size and high sensitivity, the combination of mechanical resonator and qubit could also be used for extremely precise sensing. For example, Safavi-Naeini’s team, in collaboration with physicist Michael Roukes’ team at Caltech, is already pursuing use of this platform to detect and identify proteins within cells.

Everyday technologies could benefit as well. Sound is integral to smartphones and many other devices, and this advance could be a step toward the next generation of these items, said Szakiel, a current doctoral student in Safavi-Naeini’s lab.
“This shows we can have incredibly fine-tuned control of sound, which might mean that devices that use sound as a fundamental technology can get much better,” he said.
For more information
Safavi-Naeini is also a member of Stanford Q-FARM and Bio-X.

Additional Stanford co-authors include David Schuster, the Joan Reinhart Professor and professor of applied physics in H&S; Shannon Harvey, a scientist with SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory; Mihir Pendharkar, physical research scientist at the Edward L. Ginzton Laboratory; former applied physics doctoral scholar Rachel Gruenke-Freudenstein; and Oliver Hitchcock, Matthew Maksymowych, and Kaveh Pezeshki, doctoral scholars in applied physics.

This research received support from Amazon Web Services Inc., the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, the Office of Naval Research, the National Science Foundation, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, and the U.S. Department of Defense.
Safavi-Naeini and Schuster are both Amazon Scholars.
This story was
originally published
by Stanford School of Humanities and Sciences.
Media contact:
Sara Zaske, School of Humanities and Sciences: 510-872-0340,
szaske@stanford.edu

body: What if your future self could give you some advice – or at least a little assurance – as you begin your Stanford journey?

In a panel discussion moderated by Provost Jenny Martinez during New Student Orientation for the Class of 2030 and transfers, faculty members who also attended Stanford as undergraduates shared their insights with new students on taking advantage of the opportunities Stanford has to offer and making the most of their time on campus.
Keep an open mind
The first steps on your Stanford journey may not lead where you imagined they would.

“When I was in your shoes, I really didn’t know what I wanted to do here at Stanford,” recalled psychology Professor Jeanne Tsai, ’91. She was interested in human behavior and thought medical school was where she could study it. She began her Stanford journey on a pre-med track.
“I didn’t love it,” Tsai admitted. “Pre-med classes were pretty much kicking my butt.”
When
Albert Hastorf

, a pioneer in social psychology, delivered a series of guest lectures in her human biology class, Tsai found herself drawn in a new direction. “I had no idea that you could use scientific methods to study human behavior, so that was completely eye-opening for me.”

Tsai spent the following quarter exploring what the psychology department had to offer. “I never looked back,” said Tsai. She is now the Dunlevie Family Professor in the Department of Psychology in the
School of Humanities and Sciences
(H&S), where she runs
her own lab
The panelists pose with NSO student coordinators and Stanford Football General Manager Andrew Luck. | Aaron Kehoe
Take advantage of access to experts
Stanford is full of opportunities to learn from leaders at the top of their field, panelists noted – and in some instances, from faculty who pioneered new disciplines of study, which was what
Mehran Sahami
, ’92, MS ’93, PhD ’99, experienced when he took a class on decision-making taught by
Ronald Howard
, a seminal figure in the field of decision analysis.
“It really, in a fundamental way, changed how I make decisions in the world,” Sahami reflected.

Howard showed Sahami what the field was capable of, but also its limitations – a lesson in humility, which was also illuminating for the young computer science major. “One of the things that Ron talked about at the very beginning of class, which I really appreciated, was that there are big D decisions and there are little D decisions, and you should only apply these techniques to little D decisions, which are things that you can actually analyze. Big D decisions are decisions of the heart, and those you have to make with your heart.”
Take classes beyond the scope of your major
Climate scientist
Noah Diffenbaugh
, ’96, MS ’97, shared how he took classes on William Shakespeare, Zen Buddhism, and the modern Black freedom struggle, and found them all deeply enriching.
Diffenbaugh recommends
Introductory Seminars (or “IntroSems”)

, discussion-based courses for frosh, sophomores, and new transfer students that explore a discipline in an unconventional or quirky way – which were not available to him when he was an undergraduate Earth systems major.

“IntroSems are just an amazing opportunity to be in a small classroom with a professor talking about something that the professor is, as we’ve heard, literally a world expert in,” said Diffenbaugh, a professor of Earth system science in
the Doerr School of Sustainability
Don’t be intimidated by faculty
All on the panel encouraged going to office hours as a way to get to know Stanford faculty – which they acknowledged can feel daunting. A little bit of courage helps.
“Don’t be afraid of your professors,” Kathryn Lum, ’04, urged.

Say hi when you see them on campus, Diffenbaugh said. And, if you are unsure about starting a conversation, Sahami has a tip guaranteed to get any teacher talking: “Five words, remember them. They’re easy: ‘Tell me about your research,’” Sahami said.
Find mentors

“Mentorship has been really important to me in my journey, both as a student and now as a professor,” said Lum, who grew up in the Bay Area and began college on the East Coast. But when her father became ill and passed away soon after, Lum transferred to Stanford to be closer to home. “It was really hard for me my first year, actually both years here, honestly,” Lum said. “I found faculty mentors who really helped me navigate through that, not just academically, but also at a personal level.”

Faculty are not the only people who can mentor you: TAs, graduate students, and postdocs can also become a trusted person to turn to for advice. “It’s also important to remember that one mentor isn’t going to address all the guidance that you need in your life,” said Tsai. “There might be some people who you ask more about personal things, and other people who you ask more about professional things.”
Explore research opportunities
Diffenbaugh emphasized that Stanford offers undergraduate students something exceptional: opportunities to take part in research.

“The research opportunities are really special in terms of the support and the availability of faculty, graduate students, and postdocs,” said Diffenbaugh, who highlighted the many opportunities to get involved in research and independent projects through
the Vice Provost for Undergraduate Education
. Stanford also has internships and research opportunities
available to students over the summer
, Tsai noted.

It may take perseverance to find the right lab to work with, Diffenbaugh said. “But knock on a few doors, there’s a lot of openness to having undergraduates engaged even on a one-quarter basis, and then that can grow into something longer term.”
Don’t let AI shortcut learning

As you consider how to use AI, ask yourself why you are here, said Sahami. “Did you come here to get a bunch of grades, like letters from the beginning of the alphabet on a thing called a transcript, or did you come here to learn something?”
Using AI to offload the effortful work that hard, critical thinking demands risks “short-circuiting” the learning process, he said.
“You don’t build muscles by watching a video of someone else working out, which is basically what’s happening if you use AI to do the work for you,” Sahami said.

For Lum, doing the hard work is what makes learning deeply fulfilling. “Writing is, I mean it, frustrating. It can be really difficult, but it’s also incredibly rewarding to produce something by yourself,” she said.
When it comes to research, Diffenbaugh said, AI is a powerful tool for tackling complex questions with large data sets. “Machine learning is helping us to find the signal in the noise,” he said.
Go all in on campus traditions
Tsai recommends going to the “
Big Game
” between Stanford and Cal, hiking
the Dish
, and attending the Viennese Ball. Sahami suggested taking a picnic to
the Rodin Sculpture Garden
Lum encouraged students to learn about the Stanford family who founded the university: Go to the
Cantor Arts Center,
where some of
that history is on view
, and visit the mausoleum.
Diffenbaugh also encouraged students to take in new perspectives, including attending a gathering at White Plaza, which serves as a
central place on campus for freedom of expression
and where members of the Stanford community can hold events.

“White Plaza has an amazing tradition of being a place where people express themselves,” said Diffenbaugh, who emphasized that throughout NSO and their first year on campus, students will learn and develop skills to engage across differences in ways that are curious, honest, and spirited.

“Free speech is really fundamental to our mission as a university,” said Martinez in closing. “Empowering all of you to engage freely with ideas, to be curious about ideas that you haven’t encountered before, to be open to discussing even very controversial topics is something that we really view as fundamental to a Stanford education.”
For more information
Diffenbaugh is the Kara J Foundation Professor and Kimmelman Family Senior Fellow in the
Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability
, and the Olivier Nomellini Family University Fellow in Undergraduate Education.
Sahami is the Tencent Chair of the Computer Science Department and the James and Ellenor Chesebrough Professor in the
School of Engineering
Lum is the William Robertson Coe Professor of History and American Studies and a professor of religious studies.

title: How to make the most of a Stanford education

body: The National Institute on Aging, part of the National Institutes of Health, has awarded Stanford University a five-year, $25 million grant to establish a center exploring how
artificial intelligence
can improve life for the aging population and for people with
Alzheimer’s disease
and Alzheimer’s disease-related dementias (AD/ADRD), in collaboration with VA Palo Alto and the
Stanford
Institute
for
Human-Centered

Memory loss is the best-known symptom of dementia, but other symptoms, such as agitation, sleep trouble, and depression, can have an even bigger impact on quality of life. There are many evidence-based treatments and therapies that can help. However, getting someone the exact help they need is difficult and can be a slow trial-and-error process.
The center, to be named the
Stanford University Artificial Intelligence and Technology Collaboratory
(SU-AITC)
for Precision Health and Interventions in Aging and AD/ADRD
, is taking on this complicated problem with the help of AI.

To support clinicians, who often have limited time to assess a patient, an AI algorithm could be trained to analyze a huge amount of data about a particular person and make recommendations about which medications or interventions might help.
The center is led by three principal investigators:
Ehsan Adeli
, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences, who directs the Stanford Translational AI in Medicine and Mental Health Lab;
Feng Vankee Lin
, PhD, RN, associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences and chief nurse for research at the VA Palo Alto Health Care System; and
James Landay
, PhD, professor of computer science and the Denning Director of Stanford HAI.
Ehsan Adeli, Feng Vankee Lin, and James Landay | Courtesy Stanford Medicine

“Personalizing treatment means understanding both the individual and how their needs change over time,” Adeli said. “By connecting what we learn from the brain with what we can observe in everyday life, AI could help clinicians choose an intervention, assess whether it is helping, and adapt care as the person’s needs evolve.” Adeli, who directs AI and innovation in precision mental health in Stanford’s Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, leads research connecting AI, contactless sensing, and brain imaging to better understand changes in behavior and brain health. His work brings a foundation for measuring symptoms in everyday life and developing more personalized interventions to the center.

“Doctors have clinical experience, but they don’t have the data to guide selection of the right intervention for individual patients,” Lin said. Lin has encountered many dementia patients on multiple medications to manage their various symptoms. Those medications may come with side effects and, even worse, may not improve quality of life. There are many proven nonmedicinal ways to help, she said, but interventions like exercise and neuromodulation take time and resources. “What AI can do is help tailor the intervention based on the patient’s characteristics,” Lin said.

Landay brings leadership in human-computer interaction and human-centered design, helping connect the center’s AI advances with technology that older adults, patients, caregivers, and clinicians can use in everyday care.

The new center will fund 10 to 15 research projects per year for five years. The projects will be focused on developing precision dementia interventions that use AI to deliver exactly what an individual needs. This could lead to new wearable devices, better computer programs to help with cognitive skills, neurotechnologies that personalize brain stimulation, or contactless sensing systems that track changes in movement and behavior at home to help assess treatment response. Other possibilities include robots that provide music therapy or help a person exercise.
The center is one of five across the country funded by the same NIH program to advance the use of AI for dementia.

body: In brief
Stanford Medicine researchers built an AI system called Paper2Agent that converts scientific manuscripts into interactive agents capable of answering questions and reproducing the original research.
In a demonstration, two paper agents built from unrelated studies combined their findings to identify a previously unreported genetic connection to ADHD risk.
Researchers say agent-to-agent collaboration could eventually link millions of papers, surfacing discoveries human researchers might otherwise miss while still crediting the original authors.
Since 1665, scholarly journals have stood as a written record of scientific advancement – static words on a page, a reference written by people for other people to read. That’s about to change.
A team of Stanford Medicine researchers led by postdoctoral scholar Jiacheng Miao, PhD, and biomedical data science Associate Professor
James Zou

, PhD, designed an artificial intelligence program called Paper2Agent that turns any scientific manuscript – including the text, figures, and data – into an interactive AI agent that can chat about the paper and interact with other paper agents.

“For essentially all of human history, the way that we represent knowledge is in the form of these very passive artifacts,” Zou said. “In old times, people carved knowledge into stones, and now we type knowledge into words on pages – but in some sense pages aren’t that much better.”

Zou is programming a major update to the centuries-old practice of manuscript publishing. “This is an opportunity to fundamentally reimagine what knowledge looks like. Instead of having only passive artifacts, why don’t we convert each static record into an active embodiment of knowledge?” Zou said. Think of it, he said, like a virtual author who knows how that knowledge is generated – one that’s capable of explaining it and extending it by connecting with other papers and initiating new collaborations.
paper
describing the AI work was published Sept. 16 in
Nature
. Zou is the senior author, and Miao is the lead author.
Manuscripts manifested

The paper agents can answer questions about the work, apply methods from the paper to new data, and even engage in conversations with other paper agents. The transformation from paper to AI agent starts with a team of bustling AI “worker agents” that pore over a single published paper and any associated code and data.

But they’re not just reading the paper. The agents try to reproduce the original research from scratch. In a virtual environment, the agents simulate the research documented in the paper, and through that process, they capture the know-how a reader would otherwise have to dig out manually, from reagents needed to the experimental setup and execution.
The agents store that knowledge using something called an MCP, or model context protocol.

“An MCP lets AI essentially represent a paper PDF in a form that’s easy for agents to access, almost like a filing system,” Zou said. Each section of the paper is stored in a different folder, while the introduction, methods, results, and conclusion are all organized into a separate file that lives in a parent file of a given paper.

AI does the heavy lifting, but Zou and the other human authors still have a role. The manuscript won’t capture things like failed experiments or judgment calls behind experimental setups. So humans have to supply that context to the paper agent in conversational exchanges in which the agent can question the authors about the paper and research.
AI-to-AI collaboration

A “live-action” embodiment of knowledge can be a boon for readers of scientific manuscripts who seek to deeply understand the research, but these paper whisperers can do something even more impressive. They can talk to each other. That kind of agent-to-agent collaboration could become a vast research network – one with potential to make real discoveries.

Zou and his team demonstrated the power of agent-to-agent collaboration by converting two unrelated papers into agents. One described a tool for predicting how genetic mutations affect the genome; the other described a genome-wide association study of the risk of developing attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. With both papers spun up into agents, the two began to find common ground. The genome prediction agent applied its knowledge to the ADHD dataset and flagged a molecular variant near a gene called MPHOSPH9 that’s associated with increased ADHD risk – a connection that, according to Zou, had not been reported before.
Instead of having only passive artifacts, why don’t we convert each static record into an active embodiment of knowledge?
James Zou
Associate Professor of Biomedical Data Science

“In the past, if there are two research groups that publish two different papers, those two research groups have to somehow find each other,” Zou said. With paper agents, that overlap can surface without human legwork. Zou’s team chose these two initial papers and paired them for this demonstration, but the eventual goal, he said, is something closer to manuscript speed dating at scale: Millions of paper agents surfacing common ground among themselves and working together to produce new insights.
Checking knowledge as it’s built

Zou is careful to note that attribution still matters. Agents that extend a paper’s reach are meant to help disseminate the original researchers’ work, not obscure whose work it is. “It’s still important to attribute the final discoveries and reference them back to original papers and original human authors,” he said.

Zou also noted that the parameters under which agents collaborate – and make new discoveries – should be closely guided and monitored to ensure the agents’ collaborations prioritize safety and ethical research.

The team is still expanding what a paper agent can do, including working out how, at scale, thousands or millions of these agents might productively find each other. Right now, the team has created more than 100 paper agents, but eventually, Zou hopes most manuscripts will have an associated paper agent. “Millions of papers are published every year,” he said. “There’s enormous potential here.”

body: At Stanford’s 136th Convocation ceremony Tuesday evening, President Jonathan Levin said new students are arriving on campus at a particularly momentous time, when rapid technological change promises to transform discovery, education, and many aspects of our lives.
“I can’t tell you what the future will hold. But what I can tell you with confidence is that you are in the right place,” he said.

Thousands of new undergraduates and their families gathered at Frost Amphitheater for Convocation, Stanford’s annual celebration inaugurating the new academic year. It is one of the signature events of New Student Orientation, the five-day series of events for first-year and transfer students marking the beginning of their lives on the Farm.
The ceremony included performances by the Stanford Brass Ensemble and student soloists Anna Klein, ’28, and Kent Hippler, PhD ’28, who sang the Stanford Hymn, “Hail Stanford, Hail.”

Rev. Dr. Tiffany Steinwert, dean for religious and spiritual life; Professor Jay Hamilton, vice provost for undergraduate education; and Richard Shaw, dean of undergraduate admissions and financial aid, each delivered remarks welcoming students to the campus community.
Images by Andrew Brodhead
Stanford’s 136th annual Convocation at Frost Amphitheater formally inaugurated the new academic year.
The ceremony begins with a formal procession.
While delivering the student address, senior Bryan Gonzalez shares how he found a community on campus.
Resident assistants cheer for the new first-year and transfer students.
President Jonathan Levin shares what makes Stanford a unique educational experience.
Proud parents photograph their students as they begin their Stanford journeys.
Rev. Dr. Tiffany Steinwert, dean for religious and spiritual life, delivers the benediction.
Student soloists Anna Klein, ’28, and Kent Hippler, PhD ’28, perform the Stanford Hymn, “Hail Stanford, Hail!”
Jay Hamilton, vice provost for undergraduate education, calls on new students to find their fellow “travelers” – those who will help shape their Stanford experience.
President Jonathan Levin and Provost Jenny Martinez.
After the ceremony, students say goodbye to their families.
The ceremony brought together thousands of new students, their families, and campus community members to inaugurate the new academic year.
It’s not ‘goodbye.’ It’s ‘see you later’ 🥲.
Previous
Next
Close
Embarking on a distinctive education

In his address, President Levin reflected on what distinguishes a Stanford education and how it prepares students for a good life. A key feature is the spirit of exploration, exemplified by the path of alumna Jessica Watkins, one of 27 NASA astronauts who have graduated from Stanford. Watkins arrived at Stanford in 2006 intending to study engineering, but changed her major to geological and environmental sciences. She interned at the NASA Ames Research Center and studied how to grow plants in Martian soil, eventually pursuing a PhD. Today, she is commander of the Crew 13 mission to the International Space Station.

Levin pointed out that while many educational traditions are narrow by design, Stanford is different. “You’re embarking on a true journey of discovery,” he said. “You’ll have the opportunity to take classes and encounter new ideas across many fields, and as you just heard, to change your mind. Changing your mind is a big part of education.”

Another feature he noted is expertise. Studying at a research university means that undergraduates learn from scholars who are experts in their fields, asking questions that push them to explain their work and why it matters. “The exchange runs in both directions,” he said.

He also noted the campus experience and the opportunities presented by shared moments in dorms, dining halls, and rehearsal rooms. “You are a very impressive and wide-ranging class. But that’s not why you’re here. You’re here for who you are going to become, and much of that will be shaped by each other,” he said. “What I hope you will share and embrace is the distinctive culture of Stanford’s campus – the pursuit of excellence, the openness to ideas, and the sense of optimism. At the heart of Stanford’s culture is a belief in our ability to work together and solve problems, a belief that the future is something you build rather than something that happens to you.”
Freedom, dignity, and service

Levin closed by offering new students three pieces of advice. First, he encouraged them to explore fearlessly and with intention. Second, as students encounter people with beliefs different from theirs and ideas they don’t agree with, he urged them to ask questions and be curious rather than judgmental. “The culture of the campus is, in some ways, defined by these moments,” he said.
Finally, he encouraged students to embrace their new roles as Stanford students “with humility and with a desire to serve others.”
“Be expansive in your curiosity, in your exploration, and in your contributions,” he said. “I can’t wait to see what you do with your time here, and where in the stars it will take you.”
Related story
President Jonathan Levin’s remarks at Opening Convocation
In welcoming the Class of 2030, Levin celebrated Stanford’s culture of exploration, expertise, and optimism. “The future is something you build rather than something that happens to you.”
Space to grow

While delivering the student address, senior Bryan Gonzalez recalled arriving at Stanford from West Frankfort, Illinois. It was the farthest he’d ever been from his hometown and his family. But once he found out Stanford’s nickname is the Farm, he said, he knew he belonged.
“As a small-town boy, I know farms. On a farm, things are planted, they’re nurtured, and they’re given space to grow, and I was able to find Stanford as a place where we could all grow together.”

He recalled finding a community through off-campus adventures with friends and late-night talks with roommates. After changing his major six times, he also found an academic community while taking Professor Judith Richardson’s course on American literature, which inspired him to major in English and education. “I not only found my academic home, but a mentor for my honors thesis and a trusted friend,” he said.
“The Farm has nurtured me and helped me thrive,” he added. “As I enter my senior year, I am still in awe at the community that surrounds me and takes the time to get to know me for who I really am.”
Class snapshot

On Tuesday, Stanford welcomed 1,950 new students, 1,872 of whom are first-year students in the Class of 2030 representing all 50 states and 72 countries, while another 78 are transfer students from 65 colleges and universities, 26 of which are community colleges.
The new students arrive from small towns, big cities, and suburbs, with 13 percent from outside the United States. They speak 80 unique languages other than English in their households.

Sixty-five percent of the domestic first-year class attended public schools, and the remainder attended private, parochial, and home schools. Among all new first-year and transfer students, 19 percent are the first in their family to attend a four-year university, and 10 students are military veterans.
