description: Stanford welcomed 1,950 new first-year and transfer students on Tuesday at a Convocation ceremony inaugurating the new academic year.
title: ‘You’re embarking on a true journey of discovery,’ President Levin tells new students

body: Following is the prepared text of remarks by Stanford President Jonathan Levin at the 136th Convocation Ceremony on Sept. 15, 2026:
First-years, transfer students, and families: Welcome to Stanford!

We’re so glad you’re here. We enjoyed seeing you moving in this morning. That’s one of my favorite moments of the year. Parents and families, we especially enjoyed seeing the look of pride on your faces.

Let me start with a prediction, based on evidence, although admittedly a small sample size. I predict that you are unlikely to remember much of this talk. But you will remember the feeling of arriving at Stanford.

That has certainly been the case for me. In the fall of 1990, I flew across the country, and a blue Super Shuttle bus dropped me and my two duffel bags in front of Wilbur Hall. I remember the feeling as if it were yesterday – walking around campus in the sun, meeting a few people in my dorm who I still talk with today, and seeing my room for the first time. Some of you might wonder, have the rooms changed much? The answer is no. We call it eclectic.

I had chosen Stanford for its sense of openness and possibility, for its spirit of exploration. It did not disappoint, and that is one of the many reasons I’m still here today, and I’m so excited to see you launch on your own voyages.

This weekend I was scheduled to be in Florida to watch the launch of another Stanford explorer. Jessica Watkins arrived at Stanford in the fall of 2006. She wanted to be an astronaut. Of course, I grew up wanting to play center field for the New York Yankees, so these things don’t always work out, but in Jessica’s case, it did.

At Stanford, Jessica studied geological and environmental sciences. She was a star on the women’s rugby team – winning a national championship as a sophomore. She did a summer internship at the NASA Ames Research Center, and studied how to grow plants in Martian soil. Those experiences set her up to pursue a PhD and, eventually, to be selected into NASA’s astronaut program. Today, she’s the commander of the Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station – her second trip there. By the way, Stanford has graduated 27 astronauts, and more female astronauts than any civilian university.

I was hoping to point up at Jessica in orbit, but as often happens with space missions, the launch on Saturday was postponed. I can’t wait to be there when it happens, and maybe one day to see Jessica put her geology training to work walking around on the moon, or even Mars.
One of the reasons I love Jessica’s trajectory and was so eager to be there for her launch is that it ties into something I’ve been thinking about all summer.
This fall, I’m teaching a section of
COLLEGE 101
, a course many of you will take. It’ll be a new class for me, and different. My field is economics, so I’ve usually taught classes on game theory or innovation or how to design markets.
COLLEGE 101
is about the role of education in preparing you to live a good life.

A feature of our freshman curriculum is that we invite faculty from all across campus to teach in it. That’s why some of you will have literary scholars while others have a physicist, or a physician, or an economist who’s become a university president.
So this summer, I’ve done a lot of reading: Plato, Du Bois, Tagore, Dangarembga, Epicurus, Seneca. Tara Westover’s memoir. Mary Shelley’s
Frankenstein
Many of the readings are about what education should look like, or personal accounts of education, at different times and places. You’ll get to talk about them all through the quarter.
The readings raised a question: What is it about a Stanford education that distinguishes it from the many and varied forms of education over time and place? How will it prepare you for a good life?
I think there are three answers.

First, the freedom to explore. Many educational traditions are narrow by design: a fixed course of study, depth in a particular area. Stanford is different. You’re embarking on a true journey of discovery. You’ll have the opportunity to take classes and encounter new ideas across many fields, and to change your mind. Changing your mind is a big part of education.

My freshman year at Stanford I arrived with no idea what I wanted to study. I took a class on Eastern philosophy, a seminar on Dostoyevsky, and what for me was an incredibly challenging math class. I ended up majoring in English and math. Jessica Watkins started as an engineer and switched into Earth science.

Isaiah Berlin famously described two types of thinkers – the fox who knows many things and the hedgehog who knows one big thing. A liberal education aims to give you some of both, the theory being that judgment and citizenship require both mastery and exposure to different ways of thinking.

Second, the premise of a research university is that expertise matters, and that by putting scholars together with undergraduates, everyone benefits. You will learn from faculty who have devoted their entire lives to a field. In turn, you’ll ask questions and push the faculty to explain their field and why it matters. The exchange runs in both directions.

All of us on the faculty have experienced this. One of my favorite research projects started when one of my advisees spent his junior summer working for a used car dealership in Tucson, Arizona. The business was fascinating, and we ended up writing a paper about it. I learned a ton and I think he did too. A few years later, he and his classmates started what is by far the most successful used car company in the United States.

Third, there is the experience of the campus. As Dean Shaw described, you’re an impressive and wide-ranging class, but that’s not why you’re here. You’re here for who you are going to become, and much of that will be shaped by each other – in dorms, in dining halls, in rehearsal rooms, cheering on Stanford teams, or perhaps occasionally swimming in the fountains.

What I hope you will share and embrace is the distinctive culture of Stanford’s campus – the pursuit of excellence, the openness to ideas, and the sense of optimism. At the heart of Stanford’s culture is a belief in our ability to work together and solve problems, a belief that the future is something you build rather than something that happens to you.

You, the class of 2030, are arriving at a particularly momentous time, when rapid technological change promises to transform discovery, education, and many aspects of our lives. Even here, in a place which launched the semiconductor industry, modern computer architecture, and the internet age, no one can forecast exactly how it will unfold.

But consider the following. Suppose you were starting with a blank sheet of paper, and asked to design a place to be at the current moment. What attributes would you want? A place with the freedom to explore and adapt. A place with expertise across many disciplines – science, technology, humanities, arts, the social sciences. A place that is forward-looking and problem-solving. So what I can tell you with confidence is that you are in the right place.

The attributes that make this the right place to be at a time of change also help to explain why universities are enduring institutions. Renewal is part of our design. Indeed, your arrival is a moment of renewal, yet another reason today is one of my favorite days of the year.
So I have talked about the education on which you are embarking and why it is distinctive. I’ll finish with three pieces of advice that I like to share.

First, you have a lot of freedom and many choices – courses, activities, how to spend your time. In many years at Stanford, I’ve found that the most successful Stanford students explore fearlessly – they take a few risks, they try new things – but they also set goals and think often about what they hope to accomplish. They explore with intention.

Second, you are joining a campus where people have a vast array of backgrounds, beliefs, experiences, and aspirations. That is an extraordinary opportunity for learning but it also means you will encounter people with whom you don’t agree or ideas you find objectionable. The culture of the campus is in some ways defined by these moments. We can have an environment where people escalate into heated arguments. Or an environment where people appeal to authority or social media. Or, we can have a culture where people respond by asking questions and opening a discussion – that’s a culture of dignity. At Stanford, we want to have a culture of dignity. As a Stanford student, I hope you will be curious, not judgmental. That’s a recipe for a successful, diverse campus.

Finally, we had a legendary tennis coach at Stanford whose teams won 17 national titles. He liked to start practice by walking onto the court and saying to the team: “Sorry about the weather.” It was his way of reminding them that whatever was going on in their lives, however the team was doing, they were all in a fortunate position to be here at Stanford. You are now in such a position, and I encourage you to embrace it with humility and a desire to serve others.

As you launch on your Stanford journey, I hope you also embrace the sense of openness and possibility at the heart of Stanford. Be expansive in your curiosity, in your exploration, and in your contributions. I can’t wait to see what you do with your time here, and where in the stars it will take you.
Welcome, Stanford class of 2030!

body: Stanford Medicine scientists have chalked up a major advance in growing human brain cells outside of the human brain – and outside of laboratory glassware.
In a
study
published online Sept. 16 in
Nature

, the researchers succeeded in transplanting self-organizing bits of laboratory-grown human brain tissue called cortical organoids into mice specially bioengineered and bred so that almost all of their cerebral cortex was missing. (The cerebral cortex is the outermost “rind” of the brain, to which much of our higher-level functioning such as cognition, language, attention, and decision-making is attributed.)

The resulting vastly enlarged cavity in the mice’s brains proved to be a hospitable environment. The human tissue survived, thrived, grew – and developed working connections to the mice’s brain and beyond to the spinal cord.
“These animal models offer a unique opportunity to study how disease-associated alterations in human brain circuitry manifest in an intact nervous system,” said
Sergiu Pasca
, MD, the Kenneth T. Norris, Jr. Professor II of
Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences
and a member of the
Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute
The researchers were astonished to find, in these mice, an important nerve-cell type that hasn’t been previously glimpsed in laboratory culture and has been seen only in autopsied human brains.

Pasca, who is the Bonnie Uytengsu and Family Director of the Stanford Brain Organogenesis Program, a CZ BioHub Investigator, and a science fellow of the Hoover Institution at Stanford, is the study’s senior author. Lead co-authorship is shared by postdoctoral scholar
Konstantin Kaganovsky
, PhD; assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences
Kevin Kelley
, MD, PhD; neurosurgery instructor
Tilo Gschwind
, PhD; and medical student Paul Harary.
The burden of severe neurodevelopmental disorders

The new methodology should speed research into the underlying biological causes of schizophrenia, epilepsy, profound autism, and cerebral palsy, Pasca said. “Neuroscientists will be able to learn much more about the causes and mechanisms of neurodevelopmental and pregnancy-incurred disorders and to test possible interventions to correct or prevent them.”

Such conditions are exceedingly difficult to study at the molecular and cellular level because the brain is more complex than any other organ and because living human brain tissue is nearly always inaccessible.

One in 20 American adults is troubled by a severe psychiatric illness; the associated medical, social, and economic burdens are huge. More than 1 in 100 adults suffers from schizophrenia, believed to be largely the result of brain-circuit abnormalities predating birth. Some 1% of all people remain epileptic throughout adulthood.
5% of American adults have a severe psychiatric illness. One in 218 American children have profound autism.

According to Alison Singer, president of the Autism Science Foundation, a patient-advocacy group that funds autism research, one in every 218 American children meets the criteria for profound autism: an unarguably disabled state requiring round-the-clock supervision to ensure safety, as well as assistance with activities of daily living such as getting dressed, using the bathroom, and preparing food.

“Profoundly autistic patients have pronounced cognitive disabilities, with measured IQs below 50. They are vulnerable to sleep disorders, epilepsy, and self-injury; they are disproportionally likely to exhibit aggressive behavior,” she said.

In their laboratory-generated “xenocortical” mice, the researchers were also able to show human cerebral nerve cells’ singular vulnerability to oxygen deprivation – known to be a cause, when it occurs during pregnancy or around birth, of cerebral palsy, which affects 3 in 1,000 Americans and is a risk factor for epilepsy and autism.
“While animal models have been extremely helpful, some biological features seem to be uniquely human,” Pasca said.
He and his colleagues have circumvented that constraint via a series of extraordinary laboratory leaps. More than a decade ago, they
described

the creation of what are now known as organoids, three-dimensional laboratory cultures resembling specific regions of the brain. They transformed human skin cells into stem cells that can differentiate into most of the body’s cell types, then gently coaxed these cells to form self-organizing clusters of brain tissue whose internal architecture closely resembled that of circuitry found in the cerebral cortex.
“We can now generate a broad range of brain cell types, present throughout the developing human nervous system,” Pasca said.

Various organoids mimicking distinct brain regions can be juxtaposed to spur interaction between them and interpenetration of their component nerve cells, or neurons, to form complex signaling circuits resembling those in the human brain. These
fused multi-organoid combos
, which Pasca later named
assembloids
, could be connected in threes or even fours to re-create pathways in our bodies that drive movement or sensation.

But there were limits. “We couldn’t study complex human behavior in a dish,” Pasca said. In addition, the absence of blood supply, immune-cell infiltration, connections to sensory input and motor output, and failure of some component cell types to fully mature put a cap on what could be learned from probing organoids or assembloids in culture to study neurodevelopmental disorders or human brain processes in general.
Might integrating human organoids into a living rodent’s brain – particularly when that brain was still in an early stage of circuit formation – address these limitations?
From the dish to the rodent’s brain
In 2022, Pasca and his colleagues
transplanted

human cortical organoids into newborn rats’ brains and saw much better neuronal development than could be achieved in a dish. The implanted human organoids, measuring perhaps one-fifth of an inch in diameter when transplanted, occupied a full one-third of the hemisphere of the rat brain six months later. At eight months, individual neurons from the human organoids in the rat brains were substantially bigger and more electrically active than those in the organoids – generated the same way, at the same time – that remained in a dish instead of being transplanted. They exhibited much more sophisticated branching patterns. And they integrated with their rat-neuron neighbors to form working brain circuits.

“The cells we implant carry the genetic material of the person they’re derived from – whether that person is a patient or a healthy individual – allowing us to study downstream disease effects in brain cells and circuits,” Pasca said.

“The idea that you can make an organoid model with an individual’s unique genetic character and use that to learn what’s gone awry in that individual’s brain is a critical step toward precision medicine,” said Singer, the Autism Science Foundation president.
While animal models have been extremely helpful, some biological features seem to be uniquely human.
Sergiu Pasca
The Kenneth T. Norris, Jr. Professor II of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences

In that same 2022 study, Pasca’s team seeded neonatal rats’ cortical regions with brain tissue from young patients with a rare but devastating genetic condition called Timothy syndrome, characterized by severe autism and heightened vulnerability to epilepsy and schizophrenia. Pasca and his colleagues were able to pinpoint the disorder’s molecular defect and, later on, found a candidate drug to treat it. That drug is now in preparation for entering phase 1/2 safety trials.
Even then, there were limits: For example, the rat neurons developed much more quickly than the human neurons did.
“The two parallel developing systems are in competition for turf,” Pasca said.
The advent of apallial mice

In the new study, Pasca’s team came up with a way to eliminate much of that competition. They produced a laboratory mouse strain that was genetically engineered so that the “starter cells” that give rise to the evolutionarily more-recent addition to the cerebral cortex – the neocortex – and certain other brain structures can’t get formed.

Achieving this necessitated several technically challenging steps. But the team finally generated mice that survived in healthy condition, despite the absence of most of their cortex and hippocampus, a brain structure important for memory formation.

Upon reaching adulthood, the brains of the “apallial mice” (so named because the missing cortical tissue develops from a prenatal brain structure called the pallium) contained a mere 2% of ordinary mice’s equivalent cortical content, leaving plenty of space that could have been occupied by human cortical cells.

“Our findings suggest that, when cortical circuitry is lost very early in development, the cortex may not be solely responsible for all of the functions traditionally attributed to it,” Pasca said. “Other brain regions may compensate for some of the missing cortical circuitry as the brain develops.”

While pretty much indistinguishable from normal mice at first glance, the apallial mice did exhibit minor but measurable behavioral quirks: a slightly more cautious gait, probably reflecting somewhat compromised fine-motor coordination, and a tendency to be more forgetful about recently encountered novel environments. Their behavioral performance also varied more from one individual to the next than normal control mice’s did, suggesting that the cortex has a stabilizing role in brain function.
A more complete model

Newborn apallial mice served as recipients for human cortical organoids. About two months after developing cortical organoids (derived from healthy donors who had consented to having their cells transplanted into animals), the investigators surgically positioned organoids (typically more than one per recipient) containing perhaps 100,000 cells apiece in 2-day-old apallial animals’ enlarged fluid-filled cavities in the brain.

A lopsided majority of these operations succeeded. The human tissue survived and thrived in cortex-depleted mice’s brains. Three months after the surgical procedure, more than 90% by volume of the cortical tissue in the mice’s brains was human. Integration of human and mouse neurons into circuits was proceeding apace.
Three to six months after the transplant surgery, the xenocortical mice’s performance on behavioral tests was generally similar to that of their same-age normal peers.
Stanford Medicine

In a proof-of-concept experiment demonstrating how these mice can be used for studying disease, xenocortical mice were exposed to five hours of low oxygen. The exposure wreaked substantial damage on their human-originated cortical tissue. Oxygen-deprived xenocortical mice appeared to have trouble sustaining a steady gait and maintaining their balance, reminiscent of what is seen in children with cerebral palsy. In contrast, normal and apallial mice were virtually unaffected.

“Finding out what accounts for this difference could yield clues about human neural susceptibility to oxygen deprivation, shed light on mechanisms underlying cerebral palsy, and provide a platform for testing potential therapeutic strategies,” Pasca said.
Spotted: A seldom-glimpsed brain-cell type

Remarkably, the xenocortical mice’s human brain tissue contained detectable numbers of what the researchers determined were von Economo neurons, or VENs. These nerve cells are peculiar in several ways: They’ve previously been observed only in postmortem brain tissue, haven’t previously been generated in culture, and hadn’t turned up in the earlier transplant experiments under more crowded conditions in recipient rodents’ brains. They’re very rare, accounting for roughly one in every 90,000 cortical neurons. Originally thought to be human-specific, they’re now known to be present in other large-brained, highly social animals including great apes, elephants, dolphins, and whales. In humans, they’re situated in the fronto-insular cortex and anterior cingulate cortex, two brain regions involved in social awareness and decision-making. Their projections can extend well beyond these cortical centers. They’re gigantic – much bigger than most other neurons – and distinctively cigar-shaped.

“This cell type appears to be particularly vulnerable in frontotemporal dementia, a neurodegenerative disorder that can begin in midlife,” Pasca said. “In some forms of the disease, these cells are markedly reduced, and early symptoms can include changes in social behavior and personality or difficulties with language, often before prominent memory problems emerge.”

VENs can’t be made in laboratory culture. “Yet here they were, sitting in the xenocortical mice’s human tissue. Now we can generate these rare cells from a healthy person and study them in a living, behaving animal to learn more about what they’re doing. Or we can derive cells from patients with frontotemporal dementia – or other neurological conditions – transfer them into these mice, test the animals for cellular or circuit-level correlates of behavioral disability, and then screen therapeutic candidates.”
Pasca stressed the importance of remaining within
ethical boundaries

drawn by reflection on this research: “Throughout several years of experimentation, we have received input from ethicists, neurobiologists with expertise in primate and human cortical biology, patient advocates, philosophers, and legal scholars.”
In November 2025, Pasca organized a conference in Asilomar, California, to debate the ethical implications of using human stem cell models and their transplantation.
“An overriding argument questioned the ethics of
not

conducting this research in the face of the suffering of hundreds of millions of people afflicted with neurological disorders that today are uncurable but tomorrow could yield treatments we discover by using this model,” he said.
For more information

Stanford University’s Office of Technology Licensing holds patents for the generation of cortical organoids. Pasca is listed as an inventor. The office also holds a provisional patent application for transplantation of organoids, with Pasca, Kelley, and three other study co-authors as inventors.
A researcher from the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language in Spain contributed to the work.

body: In brief
Stanford researchers developed an AI model called TranscriptFormer, trained on gene expression data.
The model allows scientists to compare cell types across species, helping reveal evolutionary relationships such as which sponge cells most closely resemble neurons found in other animals.
Researchers say the tool could help identify cell types in new species, distinguish healthy from diseased cells, and eventually guide the design of new cell-based treatments.
Researchers at Stanford University have developed two new
artificial intelligence

models of the biological cell. The first, called universal cell embedding, paved the way for a second-generation model called TranscriptFormer, which has been trained on data from 112 million cells representing 12 species, ranging from single-celled yeast to humans.
The AI cell models make it dramatically easier to compare cells among species – and offer possibilities for new insights on diseases and paths to new cell treatments.
“We’re trying to open up a whole new way to think about cell biology,” said
Stephen Quake
, PhD, a professor of
bioengineering
. He is co-senior author, along with
Jure Leskovec
, PhD, a professor of computer science, and Theo Karaletsos, PhD, of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, of two scientific articles about the work, published recently in
Nature
and
Science
. “These papers mark the beginning of, we hope, a whole new field and a decade of work,” Quake said.
The genome contains the instructions for life, but these days many biologists focus on gene
expression –
that is, which genes a particular cell is using.

For example, a beta cell in the pancreas expresses the gene for insulin, plus genes related to storage and release of the hormone. The white blood cells known as B cells produce antibodies to fight disease. A cell in your skin, on the other hand, might express genes to make hair or pigment. These differences in expression can be used to tell cell types apart. Healthy and sick cells also have different gene expression patterns, as do cells from different species.

In recent years, scientists have built various atlases, which are databases that define cells and tissues based on their gene expression patterns. The amount of data on tens of thousands of genes for hundreds of millions of cells – from many species – is staggering.
Too much for human brains

“How do we think about all these genes at once? The human brain can’t,” Quake said. “These models help us do that. The algorithms are ways for us to understand very complex data that humans can’t wrap our minds around.”

TranscriptFormer was trained on 12 species. In addition to humans and yeast, the team used cell atlases for mice, rabbits, chickens, zebrafish, fruit flies, the African clawed frog, the parasite that causes malaria, a sea urchin, a sponge, and the roundworm
Caenorhabditis elegans

The training worked on gene expression profiles, in a way that is analogous to large language models like ChatGPT. LLMs are trained, in essence, by repeatedly looking at texts with some words missing, and adjusting their parameters until they are able to correctly predict the missing words. TranscriptFormer did the same, but with gene expression values instead of words.

Quake describes the resulting model as a “universal space” – not a physical place, but a mathematical space that can be used to measure how similar or different things are. “All the cells of every organism on Earth can sit in that space, and you can look at their relationship to each other,” he said.
We’re trying to open up a whole new way to think about cell biology.
Stephen Quake
Professor of Bioengineering

One use for TranscriptFormer is to explore evolutionary relationships between different species. For example, scientists who study sponges have wondered which kind of cell in a sponge is most closely related to a neuron in other animals. The model showed that the cell known as a choanocyte was quite similar to neurons in the roundworm and the frog. This helps scientists understand the evolution of neurons and the role of choanocytes in sponges. The sponge’s neuroid cell, on the other hand, was named that because it has some neuron-like features – but it turns out to have a gene expression profile more like a frog gland, suggesting that it may instead be involved in digestion.

Another use is with new species; if given gene expression data for a species it wasn’t trained on, TranscriptFormer can identify the cell types. The team also showed that it can tell the difference between healthy and diseased cells.
Someday, the model could help guide the design of new treatments that use cells, for example – because it can imagine functional cells that don’t exist right now.
“We hope it’s going to be a very powerful tool for discovery,” Quake said. “This is a tool to help skilled biologists think about complex problems.”
For more information
Researchers from the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and BioHub contributed to the work. The co-first authors of the
Nature
paper were Yanay Rosen, a doctoral student in computer science at Stanford University, and Yusuf Roohani, PhD, now an associate director of machine learning at the Arc Institute.

The research was funded by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the National Science Foundation, the Stanford Data Science Initiative, Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute, Amazon, Genentech, GSK, Hitachi, Juniper Networks, KDDI, and the American Slovenian Education Foundation.
This story was
originally published
by Stanford Medicine.
Media contact:
Lisa Kim
likim@stanfordhealthcare.org

body: When Anya Vedantambe visited Sodexo’s Commissary, a Union City facility that prepares over 10,000 meals for Kaiser Permanente patients every day, she was pleasantly surprised by what she found.

Vedantambe, a sophomore studying symbolic systems, was expecting standard hospital fare – an animal-based protein, a starch, a small serving of veggies. But on the menu that day was poha, a traditional Indian breakfast dish of flattened rice with curry leaves and chili peppers that reminded her of her childhood. “It wasn’t as spicy as it was at home, but the texture was pretty good,” she said.
Vedantambe and her teammates toured the facility as part of
Delicious by Design

(SUSTAIN 123), a course focused on nutrition and sustainability in institutional food service. The visit underscored for the students that plant-based meals at scale can be delicious – a key tenet of their approach.
Delicious by Design is one of a series of
HPH Action Labs
, project-based courses offered through the Stanford
Center for Human and Planetary Health
, a joint effort of the Woods Institute for the Environment and the
Center for Innovation in Global Health

. Each lab pairs a multidisciplinary student team with a partner organization – a nonprofit, a government agency, or a mission-driven company – and assigns them a real-world problem the partner is trying to solve.

The classes emphasize a multidisciplinary approach to solving systemic problems: Action Lab students have come from more than 10 programs, including Earth systems, public health, engineering, design, international policy, and the Graduate School of Business, according to
Katie Vogelheim
, education advisor at the Center for Human and Planetary Health.

“While I’ve taken other courses that task students with tackling sustainability challenges, most of the projects I’ve done have been theoretical, ending in a research paper or poster,” said Riya Bhatia, a junior studying Earth systems and a student in the
Delicious by Design
Action Lab. “I was drawn to this class because of the opportunity to collaborate with a real-world partner to create recommendations that might meaningfully improve their work.”
Different problems, same approach

Class topics have varied widely. In spring 2024, students worked directly with Indonesian government officials to develop policy strategies for integrating seafood into diets. In fall 2024, students worked with rural clean energy advocates in Missouri and Wisconsin to build health impact assessments of fossil fuel dependence in rural communities – finding that fossil fuel plants in Missouri alone generate an estimated $1.6 billion in annual health-related costs. In winter 2026, an Action Lab course partnered with the nonprofit Conservation International to explore how biochar, a coffee farming waste product, could be used to improve soil health, capture carbon, and support farmers in Colombia.
I was drawn to this class because of the opportunity to collaborate with a real-world partner to create recommendations that might meaningfully improve their work.
Riya Bhatia
Junior, Earth Systems

For Ava Mae Bakhshandehpour, a freshman studying economics and a former biochar Action Lab student, the experience didn’t end when the quarter did. She went on to pursue independent research with Kate Maher, a professor of Earth system science in the Doerr School of Sustainability and one of the course’s instructors, analyzing sustainability frameworks across nine major coffee companies.
“After this class, I realized I wasn’t done working on this problem,” she said.
Taking on hospital food
This spring, the
Delicious by Design

Action Lab course turned its attention to hospital food. Working with Greener By Default, a behavioral science consulting firm, the two student teams spent the quarter interviewing more than 35 stakeholders – from hospital CEOs to food service workers – to understand why plant-based foods are lacking in institutional foodservice, despite clear evidence for nutritional and cost-saving benefits.

They presented various recommendations to Greener By Default: One student team identified  “non-select” meals, which are chosen for the patients, as an opportunity for switching to plant-based meals. The other team built an interactive tool – “the CustYUMizer” – to help hospital executives visualize the cost, emissions, and patient satisfaction impacts of shifting their menus toward more plant-forward options.

“The students did an excellent job absorbing the nuances and complexities of this work in a very short time period,” said Heidi Fritz, healthcare director at Greener by Default. Fritz said she hopes to incorporate several of the student recommendations into Greener by Default’s future work and anticipates continued opportunities to partner with the course’s faculty team.
For students who are used to the theoretical, Action Labs offer something most courses don’t: a chance to bring the real world into the classroom and test theory against reality.
“I began to understand how to zoom out, look at and across systems, and identify those impact-maximizing, constraint-minimizing places for change,” said Bhatia.
Related story
Action lab informs policies on blue food
In two courses during winter and spring quarters, student groups developed reports on incorporating fisheries and aquaculture into Indonesia’s national development strategy.
For more information

Human and Planetary Health Action Labs are offered through the Center for Human and Planetary Health, a joint initiative of the Woods Institute for the Environment at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability and the Center for Innovation in Global Health at the School of Medicine.
Delicious by Design
(SUSTAIN 123) was taught by Christopher Gardner, Tamiko Katsumoto, Sara Damore, and Katie Vogelheim.
This story was
originally published
by Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment.

body: In brief
Researchers are prototyping filters and sensors on firetrucks that provide real-time measurements of temperature, humidity, and toxic gases for first responders.
The devices also estimate the risk of exposure to toxic metals, helping firefighters make decisions such as which protective gear to wear.
With support from the Stanford Sustainability Accelerator, the team is collecting smoke samples and training a computer model to forecast the distribution of airborne metals.
The researchers aim to distribute truck-mounted sensors and filters to firefighters across the U.S. and make a smoke toxicity forecast publicly available within two years.
In early July 2026, Stanford postdoctoral researcher
Alex Honeyman
and graduate student
Mark Leone
attached a box the size of a briefcase to a firetruck in Colorado that was about to be dispatched to a wildfire 300 miles away.

The box held a prototype array of air filters and satellite-linked sensors developed by Honeyman and Stanford colleagues to collect smoke samples and measure temperature, humidity, and toxic gases like carbon monoxide around the truck.

The devices provided the firetruck’s crew with real-time data through a smartphone app, helping them decide what gear to wear on scene, conveniently monitor data like humidity and temperature, and even calculate the probability that sparks could ignite another blaze. Developed at the
Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability
as part of a larger project called
SmokeCast
, the app also estimated the likelihood that soils within 10 miles of the fire could
release toxic metals
when exposed to extreme heat.
When the firetruck returned to their station 14 days later, the crew retrieved a cartridge of smoke samples from the box and sent them to Stanford soil scientist and biogeochemist
Scott Fendorf
’s lab, where Honeyman, Leone, and their team study how wildfires release metal particles from soil and distribute them over vast areas in smoke plumes.

Researchers at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability are studying smoke variability through controlled burns. The team is tracking metal content in soil before and after ignition, following it through the resulting smoke, and training a computer model to forecast the distribution of airborne metals. | Harry Gregory
Firefighters receive real-time data via a smartphone app. | Mark Leone

“SmokeCast is helping bridge the gap between technological innovation and practical health outcomes for firefighters and the public,” says Michael Schmitt, fire chief of Colorado’s Sunshine Fire Protection District. | Mark Leone
Alex Honeyman (left) and Mark Leone (right) monitor a drone outfitted with smoke sensors over a prescribed fire in El Dorado County, California, in October 2025. | Kristin Nesbit
The researchers aim to distribute dozens to hundreds of truck-mounted sensors and filters to firefighters across the U.S. over the next few years. | Mark Leone
Previous
Next
Close
Evidence that the soil composition where a fire burns determines whether and how much metal particulate ends up in smoke is relatively new. After the 2019
Kincade Fire
in Northern California’s Sonoma County, Fendorf and colleagues investigated how wildfires can transform naturally occurring metals that are harmless when locked away in soils into
toxic, airborne particles
linked to cancer and other health problems if people breathe them in.

There’s currently no way to monitor the metal content in smoke in real time or forecast where it will go as the plume travels, Fendorf said. Widely used air quality ratings, such as the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA)
Air Quality Index
, are typically based on the concentration of fine toxic particles in smoke known as PM2.5. “It doesn’t tell you anything about the chemistry, and that is a huge gap,” added Honeyman.
With climate change, decades of wildfire suppression, and other factors contributing to
more frequent and extreme wildfires
around the world, and smoke traveling hundreds or thousands of miles from its source, this information could help
millions of people
who now routinely experience unhealthy air from wildfire smoke.
The SmokeCast team is one of more than 110 active projects supported by the
Stanford Sustainability Accelerator
, which is based in the Doerr School of Sustainability. They applied to the program for support turning
foundational science from Fendorf’s lab
into a computer model that could someday provide a nationwide forecast of toxic metals in smoke.
Stanford Sustainability Accelerator
The Accelerator spins out sustainability solutions from Stanford to benefit people and the planet.
View all spinouts.
Gemma Guilera Ferre
, a managing director at the Accelerator who guides Stanford innovations in
climate adaptation
and large-scale
data collection

, pushed the team to consider how their research could be of immediate use to first responders. This inspired Honeyman, who spent 10 years as a volunteer firefighter, to prototype hardware – the box on the firetruck.

“What are my firefighter friends actually going to do differently on a daily basis based upon what we find?” Honeyman said. “The Accelerator team’s focus on impact brought us to realize, ‘I think what they need is information on the spot.’”

Current smoke and air quality forecasts say when the main plume is coming, “but the toxic metals are out front, or maybe already hitting you, before you’re taking any precautions,” said Fendorf, the Terry Huffington Professor in the Doerr School of Sustainability. In other words, toxic metals can enter our lungs before smoke can be seen or smelled.

To provide real-time estimates, Honeyman and the team are developing a computer model that combines data on how local geology and fire temperature affect whether and where metals are released, the distribution of smoke and how quickly it travels in different wind and weather conditions, and historical levels of smoke particle density occasionally measured by the EPA.

To fine-tune the model, the team needed more data directly from fires. Honeyman and Leone, MS ’23 and a PhD student in Earth system science, initially designed smoke sampling devices for drones that could be flown into plumes. They later realized that attaching these devices to first responders’ trucks could collect samples even closer to the flames without the need for a drone pilot to accompany fire crews.

In fall 2025, the Accelerator hosted a workshop for epidemiologists, firefighters, government officials, and others to learn about SmokeCast. Among the participants was Honeyman’s former fire chief, Michael Schmitt of the Sunshine Fire Protection District in Boulder County, Colorado. He suggested which data would be most helpful to firefighters, how to recruit crews to test sensors and filters in the field, and how to make the app easy to use.
When Honeyman and Leone brought their prototype to Colorado in July, they installed it on Schmitt’s truck.

Over the next few years, the SmokeCast team aims to outfit dozens to hundreds more firetrucks with filters and sensors to continue improving their forecast, first on a regional level and eventually “getting down to exposures for individual firefighters,” according to Honeyman.
Fendorf said their goal is to have a more accurate forecast within a year, and he hopes that anyone can check air toxicity on their phones within a few years.

“We’re starting with air quality and metals and smoke,” said Honeyman, “but this may be a way to rethink how we gather environmental data more broadly and come up with practical solutions where we can verify that we’ve made a difference in people’s lives.”
For more information
Fendorf is also a professor of Earth system science, the senior associate dean for research, and a senior fellow at the
Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment
, all in the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. Honeyman is a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Earth System Science.
This story was
originally published
by Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability.
Media contacts

gemma99@stanford.edu
Monika Suhr, Stanford Sustainability Accelerator:
msuhr@stanford.edu

body: In brief
The complex properties of spin glasses inspired aspects of modern AI software. Now physicists have produced an atomic-level spin glass that can store and recall memories.
The new spin glass can retrieve complete memories from partial or degraded information, acting as an associative memory.
It demonstrated memory recall storage capacity well beyond what was theorized for a spin glass.
While a new study describes proof-of-principle work done with extremely cold atoms, the system could eventually point toward more efficient AI training and resource utilization.
A new study has demonstrated that it is possible to make a network of atoms and photons that could improve how artificial intelligence stores and recalls memories.

This network, called a quantum-optical spin glass, works as an associative memory, a form of AI that enables the recall of full memories from partial information – much like how humans can recognize a person’s face in a blurred photograph.
The advance, published in
Science

, shows that this new type of spin glass has a greater capacity to hold and recall memories than a traditional AI network of the same size. The atom-and-photon network also exhibited short-term plasticity, a phenomenon that resembles how synaptic connections between neurons in the brain change when learning new information.
“We can now make neural networks at the atomic level, and they adjust themselves in a way that is somewhat similar to how we believe our brains learn,” said
Benjamin Lev
, the study’s senior author and the Stanford Fortitude Professor and professor of physics and applied physics in the
School of Humanities and Sciences
Benjamin Lev |  LiPo Ching for Stanford University

The new spin glass was made with atoms at extremely cold temperatures trapped in a vacuum chamber, so more research needs to be done to see if it can be scaled for practical applications – but with further development, it has the potential for an even larger memory capacity.
A physics challenge
The advance helps illuminate how certain spin glasses function on an atomic level, which physicists have been working to understand for decades.

A spin glass is a type of frustrated magnet. The “spin” refers to the two states in which the atoms can orient, just like a bar magnet can orient with its north pole pointing up or down. Within a common refrigerator magnet, all of the spins align in the same direction, all up or all down, making a magnetic field that sticks it to a refrigerator door. By contrast, the spins in a spin glass are frustrated: They get stuck pointing in random directions. This is somewhat akin to everyday glass, which looks and behaves like a solid but has atoms in disordered locations like a fluid.

In 1982, physicist John Hopfield used the properties of frustrated spins in a mathematical model to show that a network of spins can store and recall information in the form of memory patterns. Low-energy arrangements of spins called valleys contain full memories. If the network receives incomplete or distorted information, it can “associate” the corrupted information with the most similar stored memory, thereby recalling the full memory.

Hopfield shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in physics for this work, which helped stimulate the neural-network research that underpins how AI computing systems such as ChatGPT process and understand language. However, the Hopfield network only works up to a certain point: When it contains too many memories, recall fails because the network transitions into a spin glass state, with frustrated spins creating an energy landscape that is too cluttered to accurately recall the correct memories.
New spin on spin glass

For this study, Lev and his colleagues overcame this problem by figuring out how to make a spin glass state function as an associative memory. The key was to make it out of atoms and photons. Using the quantum-optical effects of atoms absorbing and emitting photons, the spin glass network could still recall memories even in this frustrated state, surpassing the limitations of the Hopfield network. This quantum-optical spin glass was first experimentally realized in 2025 as described in the team’s
previous
Science
paper
, but this study took this work a step further to employ it as an associative memory.

Using laser tweezers, the researchers created an array of atomic gases in an optical cavity, a trap for light formed by two curved mirrors. Called Bose-Einstein condensates, these gases contain clusters of 10,000 or more atoms in a special quantum state, and each cluster behaves as if it were a single “superatom.”

The researchers sent beams of photons, particles of light, into the cavity. Bouncing back and forth thousands of times between the mirrors, the photons made multiple connections among the atoms, much the same way that synapses connect neurons. The photons helped to drive the spins for each superatom up or down, ultimately settling them into a low-energy valley of the spin glass.

The video depicts the new spin glass, which is created when a beam of photons (represented by green light) enters a chamber containing atoms (represented by the orange and blue spheres at center). The photons bounce off curved mirrors and among the atoms, making connections similar to the synapses between neurons. This network can act as an associative memory: When it receives a stimulus with incomplete or incorrect information – represented by the pattern at left in (a) and inset (b) – the interaction of the atoms and photons can retrieve the correct information (c). Then the full memory is retrieved, as illustrated by the fuzzy picture of Albert Einstein at left becoming clear on the right.  |  Animation by Ella Maru Studios for Stanford University
Play looping video

The team then used this small network of up to 20 spins as an associative memory. The quantum-optical spin glass showed it had up to a seven-times-greater capacity to hold and recall memories than a traditional Hopfield network with the same number of spins.
The researchers also observed that the photons could push the atoms to create a type of plasticity,
where the connections can move and change, similar to the way the human brain’s network of neurons and synapses can be rewired.

“We now have a proof of principle of a physical network that adjusts itself in a way a learning system would, and if we can improve and scale that up, AI hardware might become far less power hungry to train,” Lev said.

Since the system could allow for the storage of more memories in a small network, AI technology could also potentially use fewer resources. The research is still at a very early stage, Lev emphasized, but the team is working to develop a system with more spins, including ones that can be quantum entangled, and to investigate what other properties their new spin glass demonstrates.

“This teaches us a little bit more about how physical systems can compute, not just with the classical laws of physics, but also with quantum laws,” Lev said. “It’s great to shoot for these applications, but we're also doing this because we want to know more about how nature works.”
For more information
Lev is a member of
Bio-X
. He serves as the deputy director of both
Q-FARM
and the
E.L. Ginzton Laboratory
at Stanford.

Other Stanford co-authors on the study include first author and former doctoral scholar Brendan Marsh, former postdoctoral scholar Yunpeng Ji, and current doctoral scholars David Atri Schuller and Henry S. Hunt – all in Lev’s lab.  Surya Ganguli, associate professor of applied physics in H&S, is also a co-author. Ganguli is also a senior fellow at the
Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI)
and a member of Bio-X and the
Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute
This study also includes researchers affiliated with Princeton University and the University of St Andrews in the U.K.

This research received support from the U.S. Army Research Office, U.S. Department of Energy, Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council in the U.K., Stanford Q-FARM Initiative, Stanford Shoucheng Zhang Graduate Fellowship, and Schmidt Science Polymath program.
This story was
originally published
by Stanford School of Humanities and Sciences.
Media contact
Sara Zaske: School of Humanities and Sciences, 510-872-0340,
szaske@stanford.edu

body: Last fall, Colin Abrams arrived on campus from Maryland as a frosh and a new member of the Cardinal track and field team, balancing academics and training while adjusting to a new environment.

“Being a student-athlete can be very demanding physically and mentally, and a lot of us are coming from places far away from our parents, siblings, and the people that we typically look for that support,” Abrams said.
He soon connected with
Francis A. Pearman
, a member of the Faculty Athletics Program and resident fellow at Abrams’ dorm.

“I look at him as a mentor – someone I can talk to about anything, whether it’s school, personal, emotional, athletic,” Abrams said. “It’s important to have someone you can trust and be vulnerable with.”

The Faculty Athletics Fellows program, part of the Department of Athletics, Physical Education, and Recreation (DAPER), matches Stanford faculty with athletic programs and teams to provide student-athletes with support, mentorship, and academic guidance. Around 60 faculty members from a wide array of disciplines participate in the program, which began in 2017.

Pearman understands the perspectives of both student-athletes and faculty. The assistant professor of education played college football for the Virginia Cavaliers and in the NFL, including the Jacksonville Jaguars, Seattle Seahawks, and Tennessee Titans.

“A student-athlete’s role is one of tremendous privilege, but it also presents a host of challenges, and not all faculty are aware of some of those nuances,” Pearman said. “I feel that I can advocate for them and be that support.”
Faculty Athletics Fellows program
Learn more about how to get involved with the program
here
‘The full Stanford experience’

The Faculty Athletics Fellows program is designed to ensure that student-athletes have ample access to faculty mentorship, academic support, and research opportunities, said Meredith Basil, program co-chair and associate dean of academic advising.

“We want our student-athletes to have the full Stanford experience, as they work to balance multiple competing priorities and their unique time demands,” Basil said. “They are an integral part of our academic community, and we have incredible faculty who help us address complex challenges in support of our students.”

Stanford has 36 varsity sports, and student-athletes make up approximately 12 percent of the undergraduate population. DAPER has worked to grow the Faculty Athletics Fellows program with the goal that each team has at least two faculty members associated with it.

The program’s faculty meet quarterly to discuss issues that impact student-athletes, such as travel and enrollment. Fellows also receive invitations to all-sport activities, have free access to selected competitions, and have the opportunity to share information and raise related considerations in faculty meetings across campus.

Faculty join the program for a wide variety of reasons, said Kristen M. Azevedo, assistant athletics director and assistant dean of student-athlete success and well-being. Some are interested in sports, some are former student-athletes themselves, and some just want to support students outside the classroom.

Fellows determine what time commitment works best with their schedule, and they are assigned to a team or sport of their choice for the season. Many attend games and practices, and even travel with the team.
Chris Ayres
, the Matt Gentry Head Wrestling Coach, said having a faculty member assigned to the team sends a powerful message to student-athletes.

“Faculty fellows show they care about students beyond their performance in the classroom and that goes a long way,” Ayres said. “Our sport has a lot of first-generation college students, and having a faculty member around lets them see that professors are very approachable and down to earth.”

The fellows program also teaches the students the importance of building strong relationships beyond their peers, Ayres added. “At the end of the day, athletics, especially at Stanford, is an extension of the educational experience,” he said.
‘A bridge’
As a fellow,
Jody Maxmin
joined the Cardinal women’s basketball team in the locker room before the game against Notre Dame and cheered them on during games last winter.

“There’s absolutely nothing like being there,” said Maxmin, associate professor of art and art history and of classics. “It’s important to show up for our students, and you can learn so much about your own craft by watching others in different environments. It was fascinating.”
Maxmin, who has taught at Stanford for 46 years, said the program grows connections between faculty, student-athletes, and coaches that enrich the experiences of all involved.

“The best coaches here are models for faculty on how to challenge and correct while encouraging, and how to critique without wounding or discouraging,” Maxmin said. “And our student-athletes are models of how to stay fresh, ambitious, fit, fearless; they show us how to teach, how to take on new challenges that stretch us.”
Krista Birnie
, clinical associate professor of pediatrics, is a fellow working with the squash and women’s basketball teams. She was also one of the best 3-point shooters in Stanford women’s basketball history.
“Student-athletes are incredibly dedicated and hardworking,” Birnie said. “There’s a level of maturity and resilience that is pretty unique to the group.”

For Birnie, the program is an opportunity to get to know student-athletes and stay involved in college athletics. She and her husband have set a goal of taking their family to a game in every Stanford sport.

“It can be challenging for student-athletes to get the ‘normal’ student experience because you’re traveling and doing your sport so much,” Birnie said. “The Faculty Athletics Fellows are a bridge to help support the student-athletes, to advocate on behalf of their experience, and also for students to understand what faculty are hoping for, too.”

body: In brief
Stanford GSB researchers are building frameworks that keep AI under human control even as they become more autonomous.
In a cooperative game, an AI agent learns when to check in with a person and when to act alone.
Another framework sets up effective oversight of an untrusted model by pools of human or AI supervisors.
William Overman began his PhD program at
Stanford Graduate School of Business
at an auspicious moment: just two months before ChatGPT publicly launched in November 2022, exploding the widely held understandings of what machines are capable of.

Even as Overman began enlisting AI for his research, he grew wary of where the technology was headed. “This isn’t only about the apocalyptic potential of what could happen; I’m also thinking a lot about the future of human flourishing,”
Overman
says. He fears that misaligned AI could overstep its bounds – not necessarily maliciously – and inflict subtle, yet real, harms on people.

“To prevent that, we need to get this right,” Overman says. “We must set up the proper interactions and training and incentives for these AI agents and models. It’s critical to think about shaping all of that now, so that these tools help make life better for us, not worse.”

To think through the AI architecture that could help to ensure this balance, Overman enlisted his technical toolkit, calling on game theory, reinforcement learning, and causal inference. He partnered up with
Mohsen Bayati
, his advisor and a professor of operations, information, and technology at Stanford GSB.
Overman and Bayati have co-authored two recent papers focused on a single question: As AI systems become capable of acting on their own, how do humans stay meaningfully in control?
We must set up the proper interactions and training and incentives for these AI agents and models. It’s critical to think about shaping all of that now.
William Overman

The papers approach the question from two directions. One demonstrates how to design a relationship between a person and an AI agent from scratch, so the agent’s drive toward independence never comes at the human’s expense. The other paper offers a more practical framework that can be used with an AI system a user didn’t build and doesn’t fully trust.

“There’s a theoretical component at the core of this that is very important,” Bayati says. “We’re developing frameworks to think about two classes of problems: collaboratively building a safe AI, and controlling a potentially unsafe but very powerful one.”
Learning from avoiding lava
In the first paper, titled
“The Oversight Game,”

the researchers modeled the relationship between a person and an AI agent as a game without a winner or a loser. “It’s more like cooperative party games, where you’re trying to accomplish something together,” Overman says. “It’s not like the AI is trying to beat the human, or vice versa.” Self-driving cars are a version of this idea: Each car is trying to reach its own destination, but all the vehicles on the road share an overriding interest in avoiding collisions.

In the game Overman and Bayati designed, an AI agent can choose between two moves at any moment: Act autonomously, or defer to a human who can override its action or shut the AI agent down. The human player simultaneously chooses whether to trust the AI’s judgment or step in. Intervention is possible only when the AI defers and the human chooses to oversee. The overarching goal: Train the AI agent to recognize for itself the right moments to pause and ask the human for guidance.

The researchers tested this setup in an environment called Lavaland, a grid the AI agent must cross to reach a goal. However, the AI agent was never trained to recognize the patches of lava placed in its path. Left on its own, the AI agent would choose a route straight through the lava, triggering a steep penalty.

Over repeated attempts, the AI agent and the human learn, independently and without being told to coordinate, when to defer and when to intervene. The AI agent learns to ask for guidance as it nears lava; the human learns to step in and pick a safe (if not always optimal) way around it. (Deferring and overseeing incur a small cost, discouraging either player from overrelying on the other.) When there’s no danger, the agent defaults to acting freely and the person defaults to trusting the AI.

It’s significant that intervention comes with a cost, Bayati explains. He points to a similar situation in a health care setting. If an AI assistant is meant to help a doctor save time by taking over rote tasks, it’s costly for it to ask for oversight too often, because it burns the doctor’s time. But it’s also costly to act autonomously too often, because that can lead to mistakes.

The shared goal for both AI and human players in the Oversight Game is to settle into an equilibrium of trusting and double-checking at the right moments. That shared stake led to a useful finding: When they play the game by the rules, the two players settle into a stable pattern where the AI’s push toward greater autonomy can never come at the human’s expense.
We’re developing frameworks to think about two classes of problems: collaboratively building a safe AI, and controlling a potentially unsafe but very powerful one.
Mohsen Bayati
The Carl and Marilynn Thoma Professor

The payoff wasn’t just theoretical. In the researchers’ tests with frontier models for agentic coding, the AI learned on its own to ask for a check-in before taking risky actions, while the human learned when it was safe to step back.

“That’s what we set up this game to allow: the human and AI both learning when those critical points are,” Overman says. “If the AI has to ask for oversight at every moment, it might as well not be autonomous. But we do want to make sure that, at very critical points, it knows to ask.”
Oversight without trust
Overman and Bayati’s
second paper

takes on a messier yet more common situation: overseeing an AI that you didn’t design. “Imagine there’s a company that wants to use an open-source AI model that was built by an entity they don’t fully trust,” Bayati says. “But they want to use it, because the AI is very powerful; its performance is off the charts.”
If you can’t retrain the model, and you can’t redesign the role it’s playing, what should you do? The researchers’ response: You watch it.

Their method, which they call calibrated collective oversight, pools several weaker, imperfect human or AI overseers – none strong enough to trust alone – and uses them to collectively rein in the stronger AI system.
Critically, the researchers can mathematically guarantee the rate of bad outcomes will stay below whatever threshold a user sets.
“Using our framework, you can set a guarantee: There will be at most 5%, or 1%, unsafe decisions,” Bayati says. “You just tune the safety component.”

That guarantee matters, because most prior approaches to AI oversight have offered only empirical evidence that they seemed to work, not a formal promise they’d keep working as AI models grew more capable.

Bayati and Overman tested their approach on a modified software-engineering benchmark, where weaker overseers successfully held an adversarially misaligned coding agent in check. They also tested their framework on a game called MACHIAVELLI, which was built to test how AI systems trade off completing a task against acting ethically. In both cases, the rate of violations tracked closely with the safety target the researchers dialed in.

Of the two papers, Bayati sees the second as closer to real-world, practical use today. “It’s such a simple algorithm,” Bayati says. All it requires is a set of weaker systems you already trust – whether they’re human or smaller AI models.

The framework described in the Oversight Game, by contrast, needs practice before it’s ready for deployment. The AI and the human have to play the “game” repeatedly in the relevant setting (whether a doctor’s office, a classroom, or somewhere else) to find their footing and smooth out the mistakes that will happen along the way.

Building those testing environments well, Bayati notes, is a significant undertaking. Still, he and Overman see their frameworks as tools others can build on as researchers and AI developers work to solve the problem of AI alignment.
For more information
Mohsen Bayati teaches
Business Intelligence from Big Data and AI
and other courses.
This story was
originally published
by Stanford Graduate School of Business.

body: I. Robert Lehman, PhD, a foundational biochemist whose research fueled modern molecular biology and biotechnology, died June 15 at his home on the Stanford University campus, surrounded by his family. He was 101.
“Dr. Lehman embodied the very best of Stanford Medicine – intellectual curiosity, scientific rigor, humility and generosity,” said
Lloyd Minor

, MD, the Carl and Elizabeth Naumann Dean of the School of Medicine and vice president for medical affairs at Stanford University. “As a founding member of the Department of Biochemistry, he helped build not only an exceptional scientific enterprise but also a collaborative culture that continues to shape Stanford Medicine and generations of researchers.”
Lehman joined the Stanford School of Medicine in 1959 as one of six founding members of the Department of Biochemistry.
“Bob was the last of our biochemistry founding faculty,” said
Aaron Straight
, PhD, the Pfeiffer and Herold Families Professor and chair of biochemistry. “It feels like the end of an extraordinary generation and scientific chapter for Stanford.”

Over nearly five decades, Lehman helped discover the first DNA polymerase – an enzyme that assembles DNA – and led one of several labs that independently discovered DNA ligase, which seals breaks in DNA.
“He was a gentleman of science,” said
James Spudich

, PhD, a professor emeritus of biochemistry. “He did terrific work on DNA ligase and nucleases that became critical to molecular biology. My students buy kits containing those enzymes, unaware that work came from down the hall.”
Colleagues described Lehman as a quiet presence: gentle, patient and genuinely interested in others. But he had an outsized scientific impact through his work and his mentorship, Straight said.
“Bob was a bright light in the department and was held in the highest esteem,” said
Gilbert Chu

, MD, PhD, professor of medicine and of biochemistry, who met Lehman after visiting Stanford Medicine in 1982. “His door was always open at lunchtime so that anyone could walk in and talk about science.”
From Lithuania to Stanford
I. Robert Lehman was born Oct. 5, 1924, in Tauragė, Lithuania, to a Yiddish-speaking family. His parents,
Herman and Anna Lehman, immigrated with their only child to the United States in 1927 and settled near Anna’s relatives in Baltimore.

Soon after arriving, Herman Lehman developed tuberculosis and spent two years in a sanatorium, then found work as a baker. During the Great Depression, Robert Lehman worked at a butcher shop while attending Forest Park High School, missing school on Fridays to work and help support his family.

In June 1943, at 18, he graduated from high school and was drafted into the U.S. Army. He served in the 3rd Infantry Division and took part in the invasion of southern France in August 1944 and subsequent fighting in France and Germany. He earned a Purple Heart and a Bronze Star Medal for heroic or meritorious service.

After the war, he returned to Baltimore and enrolled at Johns Hopkins University through the GI Bill. Lehman initially planned to become a physician, as his mother hoped. A senior-year biochemistry course persuaded him to pursue laboratory research.
Lehman earned a bachelor’s degree in chemistry in 1950 and a doctorate in biochemistry in 1954, both from Johns Hopkins University. For his dissertation, he studied viruses that infect bacteria.

In 1954, while a postdoctoral scholar at Johns Hopkins’ McCollum-Pratt Institute, Lehman heard another postdoctoral scholar explain how cells produce the building blocks of DNA and RNA at a meeting in Atlantic City, New Jersey. The scholar was from the laboratory of the late
Arthur Kornberg
, MD, at the time a professor of microbiology at Washington University in St. Louis.

Drawn to nucleic acid biochemistry, Lehman asked to join Kornberg’s laboratory. Kornberg, who had heard Lehman present his work at the same meeting, invited him to join the lab in 1955. Lehman became an instructor in microbiology there in 1957.
Lehman met

Sandra Teper, who had just earned a master’s degree in psychiatric nursing at Washington University, through a mutual friend in May 1958. “Bob made his decision about us very early,” Sandra said. “Things just seemed to click. It felt right, and it worked.”

In Kornberg’s laboratory, Lehman isolated and characterized DNA polymerase I from E. coli bacteria. He and his colleagues showed that the enzyme uses an existing DNA strand as a template to build a new strand.

Kornberg shared the 1959 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine with Severo Ochoa for revealing how DNA and RNA are built. That year, Kornberg moved most of his Washington University department to Stanford Medicine to establish a biochemistry department.

Robert and Sandra Lehman married in St. Louis on July 5, 1959, and left for California the next day. At Stanford Medicine, he became an assistant professor of biochemistry, an associate professor in 1961, and a professor in 1966. He chaired the biochemistry department from 1974 to 1979 and was named the William M. Hume Professor in 1980. He served as chair again from 1984 to 1986. Sandra pursued a career in psychiatric nursing as they raised three children on the Stanford University campus.
Building the molecular biology toolkit
In his lab at Stanford,
Lehman first studied nucleases, enzymes that cut DNA. In 1967, he and a postdoctoral scholar identified and characterized an enzyme from
E. coli that seals breaks in DNA, making their laboratory one of several teams to independently discover DNA ligase.

Lehman’s group purified DNA ligase and established its roles in copying, rearranging, and repairing DNA. Ligases later became crucial laboratory tools for creating recombinant DNA and genetically engineered medicines.
“Bob was isolating and characterizing enzymes that make it possible to glue pieces of DNA together,” said
Suzanne Pfeffer
, PhD, the Emma Pfeiffer Merner Professor in Medical Sciences. “That was essential for other faculty to make recombinant DNA. His work made their discoveries possible.”
After
Ronald Davis

, PhD, professor of biochemistry and of genetics, joined Stanford Medicine in 1971, he and a graduate student asked Lehman’s lab for ligase to test whether DNA fragments could be rejoined. “They gave us a little tube, and lo and behold, we could put the fragments back into circles and join different molecules together,” Davis said. “That was the beginning of recombinant DNA for us.”

Lehman was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1977 and served as president of the American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology from 1997 to 1998. The society gave him its Herbert Tabor/Journal of Biological Chemistry Lectureship in 2008 and named him a fellow in 2026. He also served for decades as an editor of the
Journal of Biological Chemistry
An open door, an enduring culture

Lehman participated in Wednesday Club, the department’s weekly research discussion, and became its unofficial historian. Even after closing his lab, he walked to his office four days a week to review manuscripts and discuss experiments with students.
“Bob never had an agenda,” said
Daniel Herschlag
, PhD, a professor of biochemistry who considered Lehman a mentor for nearly 40 years. “His agenda was to be supportive.”

When Pfeffer joined the department as its only junior faculty member in 1986, Lehman was chair. She recalled him pulling out her chair at her first faculty meeting and being a wonderful mentor and colleague for almost 40 years.
“If you wanted to talk to Bob, you’d just go into his office,” Davis said. Lehman was “extremely non-arrogant and very interested in everything. Never a show-off. Just asking questions all the time.”

Many of Lehman’s graduate students and postdoctoral scholars became part of his extended family, his daughter Ellen Lehman said. They remained connected throughout his life, sharing family updates and research for decades after they left Stanford.
“He had this unending curiosity about things. Even in his 10th decade, he was pushing himself to learn new things,”
Ellen said. Well into his 90s, he closely read
The New York Times
and
The New York Review of Books
and worked through all three volumes of
The Feynman Lectures on Physics

“He had a real interest in his children’s and grandchildren’s lives and ambitions,” Ellen Lehman said. “He listened to others and was interested in what others had to say,” his daughter Deborah Lehman added.

Lehman took his children on weekend “science walks” and excelled at explaining science. “He was able to make something very complicated simple, but not make it sound like he was talking to someone simple,” Sandra Lehman said.
Lehman loved opera – Mozart’s
The Marriage of Figaro

was his favorite – books, food, and travel. He and Sandra belonged to a gourmet club with Stanford colleagues for about 30 years. They traveled widely, often visiting former lab members, and reread his detailed travel journals together during his final weeks.

Lehman is survived by his wife, Sandra, of Stanford; daughters Ellen of Menlo Park, California, and Deborah and her husband Marc Wishingrad of Los Angeles, California; son Sam and wife Tracee Lehman of Fresno, California; and five grandchildren.

originally published
by Stanford Medicine.
